title: Not Just Money or Jobs: How Family and Policy Shape Heterogeneous Configurations of Urban‐to‐Rural Talent Migration Decisions?
authors: Hang Liu, Guosheng Deng, Bingling Wei
abstract: Attracting and retaining skilled individuals remains a central challenge for rural development. This study examines how push, pull, and capability conditions combine to shape urban‐to‐rural talent migration decisions in China. Drawing on a survey of 1551 respondents across six provinces in eastern, central and western China, the study applies fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine the configurational effects of urban quality‐of‐life pressures, family care obligations, rural development prospects, PA, hometown attachment and self‐efficacy. The findings show that no single condition is necessary for an urban‐to‐rural migration decision. Instead, six sufficient configurations are grouped into four broader types: family‐care‐centred configurations, an external‐attraction configuration, a need‐fulfilment configuration and a capability‐enabled attraction configuration. Family care obligations and PA are prominent but configuration‐dependent conditions, whereas urban quality‐of‐life pressures operate primarily as a peripheral contextual condition. By integrating push, pull and capability perspectives within a configurational framework, this study advances a talent‐centred account of counter‐urbanisation. The findings suggest that rural talent policies should move beyond uniform incentives and address heterogeneous combinations of family needs, perceived opportunities, place‐based ties and individual capabilities.

title: Boomerang Young Adults in Seoul, South Korea: Residential Pathways, Health and Social Attitudes
abstract: Leaving the parental home is a key transition to adulthood. However, recent sociodemographic changes have produced more diverse residential pathways such as delayed home‐leaving or returning to the parental home (‘boomerang movers’). While prior research has focused on the characteristics and determinants of these patterns, few studies have examined how various residential pathways are related to trajectories of health and social attitudes in Korea. We used longitudinal data from the annual Seoul Young Adult Panel Study (2021–2024) of individuals aged 18–34 interviewed ≥ 2 waves ( n = 4895) and identified 4 residential pathways: persistent coresidence, persistent independence, boomerang and transition into independence. Outcomes were self‐rated health, suicidal ideation, social outlook (expectations regarding Korea's future relative to the present) and perceived social fairness. Mixed‐effects models were then estimated to examine differences in levels and rates across pathways. Compared with persistent coresidence, persistent independence was associated with a lower probability of reporting suicidal ideation at baseline and slower decreases over time. Boomerang adults had lower self‐rated health and higher suicidal ideation at baseline. However, they showed greater improvements over time: faster gains in self‐rated health, a more rapid decline in the likelihood of reporting suicidal ideation, larger increases in perceived social fairness and a less pronounced decline in social outlook. No significant differences were observed for the transition into independence group. Overall, residential pathways are linked to distinct trajectories of health and social attitudes during emerging adulthood. Boomerang living reflects initial disadvantages, gradual improvements and adaptation among urban young adults.

title: Crossing Boundaries in Myanmar: Strategies of Boundary‐Making vis‐à‐vis Nativist Citizenship Imaginary
abstract: This article examines popular narratives in Myanmar that use physical characteristics, such as skin colour, to argue that certain minority groups are non‐native and originally from the Indian subcontinent, and how effectively the military junta has enforced this view. Using Andreas Wimmer's (2013) typology of boundary‐making strategies, this research examines the experiences of unofficial Muslim minorities in the townships of Mingala Taungnyunt and Tamwe, Yangon, before the 2021 military coup, as well as early coup accounts, to discuss alleged discriminatory rhetoric by the Burmese State in determining who qualifies as part of the population it governs. The analysis is situated within the Citizenship Law of 1982, which created distinct categories of citizenship, and the supposedly privileged position of the Bamar people within the official list of 135 national races, tracing incentives for both closure and strategic inclusion. A first‐glance examination of discourses from above may suggest that physical traits are used to restrict access to resources and affirm group identities, with extreme categorisation increasing reliance on markers of distinction. Yet a deeper analysis from below reveals that association and discrimination extend beyond racial or ethnic prejudice, with many individuals unaware of their friends' and relatives' ethnic backgrounds. I argue that this apparent contradiction reflects not inconsistent enforcement, but strategic ambiguity: the state's classificatory apparatus is intentionally loose, and this looseness leaves room for individuals to negotiate, contest and reshape the boundaries it imposes. This research demonstrates how individuals engage with, challenge and reshape these processes, even as local governments manipulate citizenship membership.

title: Healing at Home or Re‐Marginalisation? Perceived Neighbourhood Environment, Sense of Belonging and Mental Health of Return Migrants in Peri‐Urban China
abstract: Amidst China's transition into a new phase of urbanisation, the mental health of return migrants has emerged as a critical issue. Whether returning to rural communities offers the spiritual solace of ‘healing at home’ or precipitates a descent into ‘re‐marginalisation’ remains poorly understood, particularly in metropolitan peri‐urban villages where remembered hometowns are being reshaped by urbanisation. Drawing on the survey of return migrants in peri‐urban Zhengzhou, this study constructs and validates a moderated mediation model based on field survey data to systematically investigate the mechanisms underlying the impact of neighbourhood environmental perception on the mental health of returnees. The findings reveal that: (1) more favourable perceptions of both built and social neighbourhood environments were associated with fewer mental health problems, and perceived built environment was positively associated with perceived social environment; (2) multi‐scalar sense of belonging played a mediating role in the associations between perceived neighbourhood environments and mental health, with village belonging representing the more prominent mediating pathway and highlighting the role of emotional identification in return migrants' post‐return adaptation; and (3) migration experience moderated the association between village belonging and mental health: longer out‐migration duration attenuated the protective association of village belonging with mental health, whereas a higher host‐city tier and greater perceived social exclusion strengthened its negative association with mental health problems. This study uncovers the spatial‐emotional interactive mechanisms of psychological adaptation among return migrants, providing a robust theoretical basis and practical pathways for enhancing the mental health of returnee populations through the improvement of human settlements and community governance.

title: Checks, Balances, and Presidential Ambitions
authors: Christian Fong, Kenneth Lowande, Ayse Eldes
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between running for president and members’ contributions to the core legislative functions that impact Congress’s standing relative to the presidency. This study finds some evidence that ambitious legislators attend roll call votes and oversight hearings at lower rates, but at the same time, they are more legislatively productive, conduct just as much informal oversight and are equally informational in their public oversight. When Congress votes on an issue that affects the balance of power between Congress and the president, they are more likely to side with Congress than legislators without presidential ambitions are. These behavioral differences persist even after their presidential runs, which suggests they are not driven by a strategic effort to audition for the presidency.

title: Social learning behind closed doors: evidence from seniority voting in the US Supreme Court
abstract: We analyze the implications of seniority voting on Supreme Court decision-making. We provide reduced-form evidence consistent with justices learning from the votes of their senior colleagues as determined by the voting mechanism. To explain this evidence, we develop and estimate a model of sequential voting with social learning. In the model, justices weigh spatial payoffs against the appropriateness of their disposition and consider their preferences, private information and the choices of senior justices. We recover estimates of judicial preferences, expertise and learning and use them to assess the quality of Supreme Court dispositions relative to alternative voting mechanisms. We find that the quality of the Court’s dispositions would have improved under an anti-seniority rule, in which junior justices are allowed to vote first.

title: The institutional politics of development finance: ODA’s role in shaping subnational DFI investments
authors: Nicolas Bau, Simone Dietrich, Jing Qian, Duy Trinh
abstract: Development finance institutions (DFIs), operated by donor governments to support private sector development in the Global South, often face informational barriers when deciding where to invest abroad. We argue that traditional Official Development Assistance (ODA), delivered through bilateral aid agencies, can guide these investment decisions. Specifically, aid agencies generate valuable, location-specific, investment-relevant knowledge through their ODA-funded activities across regions of the Global South. When shared with DFIs, this information reduces uncertainty and increases the likelihood of DFI investment in those same regions. To test this expectation, we leverage an original geocoded dataset comprising investments by 12 DFIs from 12 OECD-DAC donor countries, matched with subnational ODA data from the GODAD dataset for the period 2000–2020. Our quantitative analyses reveal a robust and consistent association between ODA activity and DFI entry at the subnational level. To probe the mechanism, we conduct qualitative case studies of Germany, France, and the United States, illustrating how aid agencies and DFIs exchange information and coordinate investment decisions. Our findings contribute to a growing literature on the spatial allocation of development finance and provide new insight into how traditional ODA and national DFIs interact as part of an evolving development cooperation bureaucracy.

title: Contesting Norms and Challenging Order: Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 and the Geopolitics of LGBTIQ+ Human Rights
abstract: Uganda’s adoption of the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023 reveals significant contestation among domestic and external actors regarding LGBTIQ+ human rights norms. This article argues that opposition to LGBTIQ+ rights has become central to contemporary challenges to the liberal international order by contesting the authority of liberal human rights norms as universal benchmarks of state legitimacy. Drawing on critical IR theories of norm violation, it analyzes how external actors responded to the Act and how Ugandan state actors defended the legislation. The article concludes that political opposition against LGBTIQ+ human rights in Uganda, akin to anti-LGBTIQ+ politics observed elsewhere in the world, has become central to political critique of “the West” and the existing international order.

title: Law and Political Violence against Women in Central America
abstract: Cristiana Chamorro Barrios is a Nicaraguan journalist and founder of the Nicaraguan Foundation for Freedom of the Press, a nonprofit focused on promoting freedom of expression and public access to information, as well as providing training and support to local journalists. Cristiana was arrested on June 2, 2021, in Managua, Nicaragua, on accusations of tax evasion (International Society for Human Rights 2025). At the time of her arrest, Cristiana, a member of a prominent Nicaraguan family, had recently announced her intention to challenge Daniel Ortega in the November 2021 presidential election and was widely considered the favorite in the race. The charges against Cristiana 1 — including the vague claim of “abusive management and ideological falsehood” — though made with no evidence, disqualified her from running for office. She was later tried in sham proceedings and sentenced to eight years in prison. In 2023, Cristiana was one of hundreds of political prisoners forcibly expelled from the country and later stripped of their citizenship (Abi-Habib 2023; Confidencial 2021). 2

title: Civil Servants' Compliance with Conflict‐of‐Interest Regulation: Evidence from a List Experiment
authors: Don S. Lee, Minsung Michael Kang, Soonae Park
abstract: While regulatory governance scholarship has paid significant attention to the normative importance of ethics reform in government, empirical evidence on compliance remains scant. Drawing on insights from the social value activation model and behavioral ethics, this study examines civil servants' compliance propensity under conflict‐of‐interest regulation. Specifically, we examine how a legitimate ethics reform is associated with the voluntary compliance of two legally treated groups: those with policy implementation duties and those with frequent stakeholder engagement. The results of our list experiment with a representative sample of South Korean civil servants ( n = 1977) show that both target groups exhibit higher estimated compliance propensity with the second provision of the Act, restricted and prohibited actions, but that only policy implementation duties are associated with higher compliance propensity with the first provision, reporting and disclosure obligations. Our findings suggest that ethics reform compliance is shaped not only by formal rules and deterrence, but also by administrative role exposure, perceived legitimacy, and the value‐based dimension of civil servants.

title: The Rational Design of Space Agreements: How Bilateralism Shapes Powerful States' Design Preferences
authors: Jean‐Frédéric Morin, Philippe Evoy, Cynthia Couette
abstract: The global governance of outer space relies heavily on international agreements, yet the institutional forms of these agreements remain underexplored. This article introduces a new dataset on various design features of 952 space agreements, offering the first large‐N overview of institutional design in space governance. Building on rational design theory, this article analyzes how these design features interact with one another and with negotiation structures. Our results reveal systematic trade‐offs and suggest that power asymmetry has contrasting effects depending on the context: Powerful states tend to favor greater delegation, precision, and enforcement in bilateral agreements, while often resisting them in multilateral settings. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for both power dynamics and bilateralism, two contextual factors often overlooked in rational design theory. By making the dataset publicly available, the article seeks to foster further research on the causes and consequences of institutional variation in space governance and to advance comparative institutionalist scholarship across issue‐areas of global governance.

title: Legal Corruption in the Government: An Experimental Study on the Role of Civil Servants' Political Ideology
authors: Kee Hoon Chung, Don S. Lee, Soonae Park
abstract: Legal corruption, also known as institutional corruption, has become prevalent in the public sector, but empirical research on this subject is still at a nascent stage. Given its potentially detrimental impact on the perceived level of organizational capacity among internal members, understanding civil servants' views of legal corruption is essential. We contribute to this literature a discussion of civil servants' assessment of legal corruption in the government and evidence from a survey experiment with more than 2000 South Korean civil servants. The results of our analysis suggest that civil servants evaluate the degree of legal corruption in the government through their political lens, that is, their political ideology. Specifically, they tend to be more critical when the government is ruled by a chief executive and party that have different political views from their own, compared to when it is governed by those with the same political views. The implications of this study are clear: the central role of political views and policy preferences in understanding perceptions of legal corruption in the public sector.

title: Legislative Financial Asset Disclosure, Firm Motivations, and Macroeconomic Outcomes in the US States
authors: Justin H. Kirkland, Patrick E. Shea
abstract: Financial asset disclosure laws are widely implemented to combat conflicts of interest among policymakers, yet their economic impact remains poorly understood. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of how these transparency measures affect macroeconomic outcomes across the 50 US states. We theorize that these disclosure and recusal laws could have divergent impacts on macroeconomic performance: they might enhance economic outcomes by curtailing the exploitation of political connections by business firms, or conversely, they could impede economic growth by altering firm behavior and deterring business leaders from seeking public office, thereby potentially reducing the pool of economically savvy policymakers. Using new data on state‐level disclosure policies, we find that asset disclosure laws are associated with a worsening macroeconomic environment in states. To uncover the mechanisms driving these counterintuitive results, we conduct two pre‐registered survey experiments with 2000 small business owners. Our experimental evidence suggests that stringent disclosure requirements deter business investment and expansion. This research has implications for legislative challenges for legislative design, transparency, and economic policy.

title: Policy Window as a Trapdoor: Rethinking the Multiple Streams Framework through the Defunding of U.S. Public Media
authors: Hilde Van den Bulck, Christopher Ali, Jonathan Kropko
abstract: This article analyses the 2025 defunding of U.S. public media as a critical case to revisit Kingdon’s multiple streams framework (MSF). While MSF offers a useful heuristic for understanding policy change through the convergence of problem, policy, and political streams, its explanatory power is limited by assumptions of contingency, pluralism, and stakeholder inclusion. Under growing illiberalism, the “policy window” functioned less as an accidental opening than as a trapdoor, built through ideological persistence, institutional erosion and coordinated policy design. Drawing on critical discourse analysis of congressional hearings, executive orders, political communication, and media coverage, alongside survey data on public broadcasting system audiences, this study shows how conservative actors sustained a politicized definition of public media bias and institutionalized policy solutions. The survey highlights a disjuncture between audience trust and the construction of public media as a policy problem. Rather than spontaneous convergence, the case reflects coordinated restructuring of the public media system. More broadly, it suggests that MSF becomes less effective when stream independence is undermined by executive dominance and ideological alignment, requiring approaches that foreground power, discourse, and exclusion.

title: An Effort Made for Whom? Exploring Ministers’ Public Approval and Name Recognition in Relation to Their Media Activity
authors: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Jonas Krogh Madsen, Peter Heyn Nielsen
abstract: In many democracies, cabinet ministers find themselves in a difficult situation, juggling a demanding administrative job with political responsibilities and the need to communicate and campaign to secure reelection. With the rise of social media, this balance is becoming increasingly unstable. However, the tangible benefits of media visibility outside election campaigns remain unclear, making it difficult to determine whether such efforts yield meaningful political returns. This study examines and compares whether Danish ministers’ media activities—both in traditional and social media—impact their name recognition and popularity in the Danish population. We utilize thirty-two nationally representative opinion polls conducted between March 2020 and May 2024 and merge these with extensive records of all Danish ministers’ Facebook activity and appearances in traditional media outlets throughout the same period. Overall, our findings show that ministers’ activity in traditional media is associated with only minor gains in name recognition, while social media activity has either zero or minimal gains in popularity. Moreover, breaking down these correlations across different types of Facebook interactions and traditional media outlets suggests a trade-off between reaching and being perceived favorably by voters, showing the multifaceted nature of (social) media activity. Consequently, while we do not rule out any significant effects of social media on voters’ perceptions, we argue that social media activity is no panacea for politicians to improve their public popularity and name recognition.

title: Incivility Among Politicians: Driven by Rational Minds or Personal Drives?
abstract: There is growing concern about politicians engaging in incivility by mocking and insulting each other. While prior research often explains such discourse through rational choice, emerging work highlights the role of politicians’ individual traits, such as their personality. Yet, a unified theoretical account of how rationality and individual predispositions interact to shape harmful elite discourse is lacking. Drawing on foundational insights from psychology, we argue that politicians’ discourse reflects primarily rational considerations, which are moderated by their individual predispositions, leading to uncivil communication between politicians. We test this notion using elite survey data, unobtrusive measures of their individual traits, and direct observations of politicians’ social media communication in Belgium – a rare integration of psychological and behavioral evidence at the elite level. The results show that politicians’ use of uncivil discourse responds to rational considerations, but that the strength of this response depends on their individual predispositions. These findings demonstrate that individual traits moderate how politicians translate rational incentives into harmful discourse, providing a more nuanced account of the causes of elite incivility.

title: Narratives of Power: AI, Agency and the EU AI Act
abstract: Public debate around AI has been characterised by hegemonic narratives that delineate the scope of the conversation, suppressing different voices and limiting nuanced discussion of the technology’s harms and benefits. Scholars have identified technological or enchanted determinism, the arms race mentality and the utopia versus dystopia debate as key narratives around AI. These ideas saturate the conversation, driven primarily by the tech industry, which positions itself as the (only) expert voice. The industry’s capacity to drive these narratives is facilitated by its established institutional authority and dominant presence in public discourse, as well as the knowledge asymmetry inherent in the proprietary, ‘black-box’ nature of AI systems. Tech firms leverage the technical opacity of AI and their powerful societal position to define the contours of public debate, assigning agency to AI itself and the tech industry; constructing users and civil society as passive observers or recipients; and establishing a frame for debate that focuses on extreme consequences or hyperbolic benefits. This study, conducted early in 2024, investigates the effects of this interpretive frame on the policy choices and communications of the EU AI Act, through a mixed-methods computational and critical discourse analysis. Within EU governing body texts, the same discursive patterns that map agency and erase the middle ground of debate in AI are found, helping to marginalise alternative perspectives from other stakeholders and prevent nuanced understandings of potential harms. In the context of the Act itself, these patterns reverberate in the assignment of agentic roles and the scope of the regulation.

title: Agrivoltaics can reduce political polarization and local opposition to solar energy on land
authors: Lukas Fesenfeld, Leon Sistek, Simon Montfort, Dionis Anderegg, Jürg Rohrer, Tobias Schmidt
abstract: As solar energy deployment on land intensifies, political polarization and local opposition increasingly challenge its social acceptance. We propose that agrivoltaics – a dual land-use technology that combines solar power generation with agricultural production – can help bridge ideological divides and reduce local opposition by minimizing land-use conflicts and offering additional benefits to rural communities. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a pre-registered, field-embedded experiment with a representative sample (2145 Swiss residents) just prior to a national renewable energy referendum, combining a personalized geolocated information treatment on local agrivoltaics potential with a conjoint experiment varying key technology and project design attributes. Here we show that agrivoltaics garners broad public support across ideological groups and reduces local opposition, especially when projects are well integrated into agricultural landscapes, do not significantly reduce agricultural yields, and are locally owned. These findings underscore the importance of technology and project design in addressing local and right-leaning opposition to land-based solar energy.

title: Risk factors for major depressive disorder among adults recruited from hospital settings in Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia and South Africa
authors: Allan Kalungi, Wilber Ssembajjwe, Kester B. B. Tindi, Emmanuel K. Mwesiga, Jared G. Maina, Fred Kirumira, Elizabeth G. Atkinson, Lukoye Atwoli, Mark Barker, Lori B. Chibnik, Symon M. Akena
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) significantly contributes to the mental health burden in Africa, requiring insights into prevalence and risk factors to inform culturally responsive care. This study assessed current and lifetime MDD prevalence and associated factors among 7,073 adults from hospital settings in Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia, and South Africa within the NeuroGAP-Psychosis study. Prevalence was 0.9% for current MDD and 5.1% for lifetime MDD, substantially lower than prior estimates from the region. Lower rates may be due to the population studied or cultural variations in expression of symptoms. Multilevel logistic regression identified significant associations between current MDD and negative life events, alcohol use, and Kessler psychological distress scores, while lifetime MDD was linked to age, female sex, chronic pain, frequent headaches, and positive psychosis screening. These findings underscore the need for targeted mental health interventions tailored to the identified factors to reduce the burden of MDD in diverse African contexts.

title: Dynamic population presence linked to home neighbourhoods in the Helsinki Metropolitan Area: A 24-hour weekday and weekend dataset
authors: Kerli Müürisepp, Olle Järv, Matti Manninen, Tuuli Toivonen
abstract: In this article, we present a 24-hour population presence dataset from the Helsinki Metropolitan Area (HMA), Finland. This population-level and metropolitan-wide dataset shows hourly population distribution across HMA neighbourhoods on an average weekday (Mon–Fri) and an average weekend day (Sat–Sun), and links people’s hourly presence to their home neighbourhoods. The dataset was derived from mobile phone data, collected by a major Finnish mobile network operator in 2021, through anonymisation, spatio-temporal aggregation, normalisation, and weighting based on neighbourhood population data from Statistics Finland. The published data serve as a calibrated and validated proxy for the entire HMA population distribution. Data validation showed strong agreement between the population register data and the study population’s residential and night-time presence distribution. By linking dynamic presence data to home neighbourhoods, the dataset allows both people-based and place-based analyses, and integration with socioeconomic indicators. Moreover, its population-level scope, metropolitan-wide coverage, and capture of both weekdays and weekends makes the dataset valuable for a range of research questions and policy applications related to daily mobility, urban vitality, social mixing, green space use, epidemic modelling, and beyond.

title: Romantic love related relationships picture dataset (Love_Pic Dataset)
authors: Yudie Zhang, Shuqin Liu, Min Shao, Lu Chen, Huiling Qian, Zilong Wei, Wenbo Peng, Jing Meng
abstract: Current picture datasets lack sufficient materials to investigate complex romantic love relationships (falling in love, being single, break-up). Addressing this gap, we developed the Romantic Love Related Relationships Picture Dataset (Love_Pic Dataset), comprising 26 love, 22 single, and 23 break-up pictures. These pictures underwent rigorous validation for relationship identification, affective valence, and arousal level by 114 participants (57 females). Results confirmed distinct emotional profiles: Love pictures elicited the most positive affective valences and highest arousal levels. Single pictures evoked moderate affective valences and moderate arousal levels. Break-up pictures induced the most negative affective valences, though with moderate arousal levels. The Love_Pic Dataset demonstrates strong internal consistency, confirming its reliability. This validated resource provides an essential tool for future research exploring the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying romantic love relationships. Furthermore, it enables investigation into bystanders’ emotional reactions to depictions of these relationship states. The Love_Pic Dataset is openly available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BNVJQ .

title: “Fairness Labels” in Feeds: Process Disclosures, Provenance, and User Choice Among Short‑Video Creators in Mainland China
abstract: Algorithmically ranked feeds allocate attention in ways that can reproduce inequalities in visibility. We test whether a compact, feed-level process disclosure —a banner describing exposure-safeguard governance, paired with provenance cues and in-situ user-choice affordances—improves perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy among short-video creators in mainland China. In a mobile-first online experiment with 1,154 research-verified PRC creators in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), participants viewed a realistic feed randomized to No label , Personalization notice , or Fairness disclosure ; within the fairness condition, we factorially varied frame (Safeguards/Parity/Quotas/Exposure-fairness), issuer provenance (platform vs. independent audit), and disclosure depth (minimal badge vs. brief rationale). The compound fairness disclosure increased perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy relative to both controls and was accompanied by lower self-censorship and higher voice intentions. Effects were directionally stronger in civic/news contexts and among creators who self-identified as marginalized or previously down-ranked. Within-arm exploratory diagnostics suggested that quota-like parity framing may yield directionally lower legitimacy than exposure-fairness framing, while audit cues produced directionally positive but imprecise trust gains. Backfire checks found no implied-unfairness spillover for unlabeled items and no interaction with per-item AI-content labels, although AI labels reduced perceived accuracy. Together, these findings suggest that governance-aligned micro-disclosures can function as procedural visibility signals for creators, while underscoring the importance of verifiable claims and careful disclosure design.

title: Sharing the Alternative – The Role of Digital Platforms for Alternative News-Sharing Behavior
abstract: In a time of growing concerns over factual accuracy in the public sphere, alternative news media have emerged as a counterpoint to traditional mass media. In Germany, many online-only outlets cater to a rising audience, driven by distinct goals, standards, and funding structures compared to what they term ‘elite media’. Digital platforms are vital to their success, enabling audience growth with minimal financial investment and bypassing legacy media systems’ critique and verification mechanisms. Their reach, however, relies on followers sharing content and leveraging social media’s network effect to amplify niche information. Yet, the sharing habits of alternative news audiences remain understudied. This study uses original survey data from over 2,000 German alternative news users (collected in September 2023), exploring whether these patterns drive alternative media’s rise as a counterweight to established journalism. We investigate users’ sharing activity, their motivations for sharing news or refraining from it, and sociodemographic/ideological predictors for alternative news sharing.

title: Right-Wing Shift? Evaluating Authoritarianism, Social Dominance, and System Justification Among People of Color Before and After the 2024 Election
authors: Emily Ortiz, Ramona Alhambra, Andrew M. Engelhardt, Efrén Pérez
abstract: Non-trivial shares of people of color (PoC) have long identified as Republicans, and many of them helped cement Donald Trump’s 2024 re-election. How durable was this shift toward the political right among some PoC? We test two claims in this brief research note. First, consistent with polarization literature, we claim that partisanship primed three conservative postures among Republican PoC during the 2024 campaign: authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, and system justification. Second, aligning with work on expressive survey responses, we argue that these postures faded significantly once Trump’s agenda produced visibly harmful consequences for PoC (e.g., deportation raids; weakened civil rights). Leveraging a three-wave panel of Black, Latino, and Asian adults ( N = 3,626), our pre-registered analyses indicate Republican partisanship in June 2024 heightened authoritarianism, social dominance, and system justification among Black, Latino, and Asian adults in December 2024. These patterns were fleeting, with partisanship’s impact on these postures withering by July 2025. We find scattered evidence that these postures intensified PoC’s Republican partisanship during this period, implying our results reflect campaign effects rather than an unerring endorsement of these right-wing inclinations among Republican PoC.

title: Prime Locations
authors: Gabriel M. Ahlfeldt, Thilo N. H. Albers, Kristian Behrens
abstract: We develop a method for delineating prime locations—ultradense clusters of economic activity—within cities and apply it to comprehensive establishment data covering all US metropolitan areas. We further use big data to extend the analysis to a global context where administrative data are sparse. Many cities in the United States and around the world are dominated by a small number of prime locations that can concentrate up to one-half of tradable services jobs on tiny shares of land and are dominant centers of economic gravity. In cities with fewer prime locations, a larger tradable services share concentrates in them. (JEL C55, R23, R32, R38, R52, R58)

title: What Is Newsworthy? Theory and Evidence
authors: Luis Armona, Matthew Gentzkow, Emir Kamenica, Jesse M. Shapiro
abstract: We introduce a model in which a benevolent news outlet decides whether to report the realization of a state to a consumer, who pays a cost to receive it. A simple statistical rule, called a proper scoring rule, describes when the outlet should be more likely to report the realization. Using data from the US television news, we show that a particular scoring rule successfully predicts many salient features of news reporting. We show how to use this rule as a control variable to discipline tests of reporting bias, and we show that controlling for it matters in our applications. (JEL D83, C44, L82)

title: Pricing with Algorithms
abstract: This paper studies Markov perfect equilibria in a repeated duopoly model where sellers choose algorithms. An algorithm is a mapping from the competitor's price to own price. Once set, the algorithms respond quickly. Customers arrive randomly, and sellers can periodically revise their algorithms. The main results are that (i) for the simple two-price model with standard profit functions, monopoly pricing is the unique equilibrium outcome and (ii) for any general finite price grid, all equilibrium outcomes feature supracompetitive pricing. Sustenance of such collusion seems outside the scope of current antitrust laws, for it does not involve any direct communication. (JEL C73, D21, D43, K21)

title: Unconditional Convergence in Manufacturing: A Reassessment
authors: Berthold Herrendorf, Richard Rogerson, Ákos Valentinyi
abstract: The movement of labor out of agriculture is a central feature of the development process. A long-held view is that successful development requires that much of the labor released from agriculture be allocated to manufacturing rather than services. Rodrik's (2013) finding of unconditional convergence for manufacturing productivity, using data from UNIDO, provided empirical support for this view. We argue that the UNIDO data are ill-suited for studying cross-country productivity dynamics. Using recently released GGDC data designed for this purpose, we revisit the issue and find no evidence of unconditional convergence in manufacturing productivity over 1990–2018. (JEL D24, J24, L60, O13, O14, O47, Q10)

title: The Missing Middle Managers: Labor Costs, Firm Structure, and Development
authors: Jonas Hjort, Hannes Malmberg, Todd Schoellman
abstract: Using data obtained from human resources consulting firms, we document the cost to large firms of hiring managers and business professionals in 146 countries worldwide. The average pay in the poorest decile of countries is $18,000 per year, which is 9.7 times GDP per worker. In contrast, in the richest decile of countries, large firms pay managers and business professionals only 0.8 times GDP per worker. We use an appropriate technology model to show that the cost of management could be an important deterrent to the expansion of the modern sector in developing countries. (JEL J23, J24, J31, L84, M10, M51, O15)

title: The Missing Loan-to-Value Cycle
authors: Manuel Adelino, W. Ben McCartney, Antoinette Schoar
abstract: We show that the equilibrium loan-to-value (LTV) distribution in the US mortgage market has been remarkably stable over the last quarter century, both in aggregate and region by region, despite large, cross-sectionally heterogeneous house price cycles. While high-LTV mortgages changed from being explicitly government backed to privately securitized and back, their overall fraction remained unchanged. A repeat-sales methodology and an analysis of loan performance confirm that this stability in the distribution of LTVs holds even within subgroups of the population. These findings are inconsistent with models of credit cycles that use changes in collateral constraints to generate boom-and-bust dynamics in house prices. (JEL C43, E32, G21, G51, R21, R31)

title: How Test-Optional Policies in College Admissions Disproportionately Harm High-Achieving Applicants from Disadvantaged Backgrounds
authors: Bruce Sacerdote, Douglas O. Staiger, Michele Tine
abstract: We analyze data from one elite institution and find that test score–optional policies harm the likelihood of admission for high-achieving applicants from disadvantaged backgrounds. Under test-optional policies, these applicants submit test scores at too low a rate; they more than double their admission probability (from 2.9 percent to 7.2 percent) by reporting scores. Our findings suggest that, more than commonly understood, elite institutions interpret test scores in the context of an applicant's background. Thus, availability of test scores on an application can promote rather than hinder social mobility. (JEL I23, I28)

title: Screening Adaptive Cartels
authors: Juan Ortner, Sylvain Chassang, Kei Kawai
abstract: We propose an equilibrium theory of data-driven antitrust oversight in which regulators launch investigations on the basis of suspicious bidding patterns and cartels can adapt to the statistical screens used by regulators. Our main result establishes that screening for collusion using tests with a low false-positive rate (safe tests) is a robust improvement over laissez-faire. Safe tests do not create new collusive equilibria and do not hurt competitive industries. In addition, safe tests can have strict bite, including unraveling all collusive equilibria in some settings. (JEL D21, D43, D44, K21, L12, L14)

title: Auditing urban nature access claims for sustainable city governance
abstract: Urban governments use nature-access indicators to assess biodiversity, health, equity and regenerative-planning goals, yet policy conclusions can depend on how the claim is constructed. We audit six specifications—inventory, access geometry, distance model, threshold, population allocation and vulnerability definition—using three purposive core cities, transfer checks, a 30-city data-readiness screen and an entrance-aware London validation. Plausible alternatives changed access levels by up to 48.82 percentage points, reversed some environmental-justice classifications and substantially altered underserved target populations. A matched London diagnostic showed that network penalties narrowed from 36.95 points at 300 m to 0.52 points at 1000 m. We therefore propose a decision-stability envelope that reports a preferred specification alongside ranges, equity-direction changes, target-set reclassification and missing operational data. The cases are not globally representative; they demonstrate an auditable workflow for testing whether urban nature claims are sufficiently stable to guide regenerative and equitable planning.

title: The mentalizing network updates neural representations of romantic interest in response to social feedback
authors: Benjamin Silver, Christopher Baldassano, Lila Davachi, Kevin Ochsner
abstract: In what ways are social evaluations of others interdependent with what we think they believe about us? In the current study, we were interested in how social feedback changes how we think about a potential romantic partner, as well as how often we think about them. We hypothesized that the mentalizing network would play a role in both of these processes, given that we consider both how we feel about someone and how we think they feel about us when evaluating romantic interest. During an fMRI scan, participants watched dating profile videos of eight different targets, and assessed each target on romantic interest. Participants watched two videos of each target: one before receiving social feedback from the target, and one after. Participants also completed a resting state scan after viewing each set of eight videos. We found that the mentalizing network played a role in forming and updating evaluations of romantic interest. Specifically, neural representations in this network responded most strongly to social feedback that was incongruent with one’s initial evaluation, likely because our romantic interest in another person is at least partially dependent on how we believe they feel about us. Within the mentalizing network, the right TPJ and the dmPFC most strongly represented romantic interest at the beginning of an encounter. In addition, representations in the TPJ and the Precuneus changed more in response to incongruent feedback, while reactivation frequency in the TPJ changed more in response to congruent feedback, further demonstrating the importance of interdependence in social evaluations.

title: Digital Transformation Capabilities and Supply Chain Finance Resilience: An Integrated AI–Blockchain–Analytics Framework
abstract: Supply chain finance (SCF) plays a pivotal role in maintaining liquidity and operational continuity across global value networks. However, systemic supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic volatility, and information asymmetry frequently expose SCF programs to severe friction and default risks. While digital transformation is widely touted as a catalyst for supply chain resilience, empirical evidence regarding the explicit mechanisms through which distinct digital transformation capabilities enhance Supply Chain Finance Resilience (SCFR) remains fragmented. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), and Information Processing Theory (IPT), this study develops and tests an integrated framework evaluating the direct and indirect impacts of Artificial Intelligence Capability (AIC), Blockchain Capability (BC), and Data Analytics Capability (DAC) on SCFR, mediated by Digital Trust in SCF Platforms (DT). Using a computational research simulation methodology, a respondent-level dataset (N=500) representing supply chain, finance, operations, and IT decision-makers across international enterprises was algorithmically generated under a defensible latent-variable covariance structure. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was executed to evaluate the measurement and structural models. The structural analysis reveals that AIC (β=0.241,p<.001), BC (β=0.312,p<.001), and DAC (β=0.284,p<.001) significantly and positively drive Digital Trust in SCF Platforms, explaining 54.2% of its variance (R^2=0.542). Digital Trust, in turn, exerts a substantial direct effect on SCFR (β=0.385,p<.001). Furthermore, direct effects on SCFR were confirmed for DAC (β=0.218,p<.001) and AIC (β=0.152,p=.002), whereas the direct link from BC to SCFR was non-significant (β=0.071,p=.158). Formal mediation testing using percentile bootstrapping confirmed that Digital Trust fully mediates the relationship between Blockchain Capability and SCFR, while partially mediating the relationships for AIC and DAC. The overall structural model accounts for 58.6% of the variance in Supply Chain Finance Resilience (R^2=0.586,Q_"predict" ^2=0.412). This methodological prototype advances theoretical understanding by unpacking the granular capability configurations necessary to foster digital trust and financial resilience in supply networks. For practitioners and policymakers, the findings highlight that investing in blockchain technology yields minimal resilience benefits unless coupled with platform-wide digital trust mechanisms, whereas AI and analytics offer dual-pathway benefits across operational and relational domains.

title: Estimating Regional Industry Employment from Economic Location Mechanisms: A Constrained Spatial Disaggregation for European Geographies
abstract: Fine-scale employment by industry is largely unavailable across European municipalities, yet it underpins regional economic analysis, environmental-economic extensions, and the regionalization of input--output accounts. This paper presents a mechanism-driven, constrained spatial disaggregation framework that estimates industry employment down to the Local Administrative Unit level while preserving official totals exactly at every geographical level. The economic mechanisms that shape where activity locates --- settlement, infrastructure and accessibility, natural-resource endowments, and inter-industry co-location --- are represented as a reproducible input dataset assembled from official and remote-sensing sources; a family of constrained allocation models, combined by a cross-validated convex ensemble, is trained on data-rich United States geographies and transferred to Europe under official Eurostat totals as constraints. Validated against independent national statistics in Italy, France, Germany, and Spain, the estimates reproduce the observed spatial distribution of employment within the held-out uncertainty of the models themselves, and the error does not inflate down the four-step disaggregation. The framework is open, inspectable, and reproducible, providing internally consistent fine-scale employment estimates wherever sub-national industry data are sparse.

title: The Paperwork of Grief: Administrative Burden as a Defence Against Death Exposure in Clinical Care
abstract: Administrative work (documentation, the electronic record, the proliferation of meetings, the referral of distress onward to specialists) is treated almost universally in the clinician-wellbeing literature as a cause of burnout to be measured and reduced. This paper argues that in the most death-saturated settings of medicine (the cancer ward, the intensive care unit, the palliative service) that same burden may also do something the literature has not noticed: function as a social defence against sustained exposure to dying, offering clinicians a bounded, completable, finite task to retreat into when the bedside offers only problems that often end in death. The argument revives Isabel Menzies Lyth’s 1959 account of hospital routine as a collective defence against anxiety and brings it forward to the era of the electronic record, joining four literatures (on documentation burden, on death exposure and numbing, on terror management, and on the social defences of institutions) that have not previously been read together. If the conjecture holds, the prevailing prescription to strip administration away on efficiency grounds alone risks removing an unrecognised container without supplying a deliberate one, and the proper task is not to reduce paperwork but to distinguish what merely numbs from what genuinely contains, and to design containment for those who work among the dead. The claim is interpretive and bounded to high-mortality settings; the paper sets out how it could be tested and the competing explanations it complements rather than displaces.

title: When Does Generative AI Become a Developmental Resource? A Multilevel Taxonomy of Enactment Conditions
authors: Andreea Nicolau, Sonja Rispens, Pascale Marie Le Blanc, Kees Maton, Piet van Gool, Ad Kleingeld
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) creates a developmental ambiguity for organizations: it can support learning, reflection, and judgment, but it can also accelerate task completion while reducing engagement with the cognitive and social processes through which capabilities develop. This study asks which multilevel conditions shape whether GenAI is enacted as a resource for learning and continuous development or as a shortcut for task completion. Drawing on an inductive, multi-stakeholder qualitative study with 41 organizational actors, we use thematic analysis to identify empirical categories and morphological principles to organize them into a multidimensional taxonomy of GenAI enactment. The taxonomy identifies four interrelated dimensions: Organizational Conditions, Capability Conditions, Decision Drivers, and GenAI Enactment. Interpreting these findings through the automation–augmentation paradox, we show that automation- and augmentation-oriented uses are not fixed properties of technologies or tasks but contextually produced orientations shaped by an iterative system of societal/institutional, organizational, and individual-related conditions. The study contributes to AI and management research by specifying the condition architecture through which GenAI becomes more or less developmental in practice. We argue that learning-oriented GenAI integration requires attention to the multilevel conditions that preserve verification, reflection, feedback, and accountable judgment when task completion no longer necessarily develops capability.

title: Climate policy is domestic politics: Mechanisms shaping the political feasibility of mitigation
authors: E. Keith Smith, Christina Eder, Sarah Gomm, Gabriele Spilker, Isabelle Stadelmann-Steffen
abstract: The Paris Agreement shifted the central challenge of climate mitigation from international burden-sharing to domestic politics. In high-emitting countries, the binding constraint on near-term emissions cuts is no longer the absence of effective policy instruments, but their political feasibility, that is, governments' capacity and willingness to adopt, implement, and sustain mitigation policy over time. We review the political feasibility of climate mitigation along four dimensions: stakeholder interests and influence, public opinion and social norms, political-economic context and institutional constraints, and distributional effects and inequality. Using the policymaking process as our analytical lens, we trace how these dimensions hinder or enable mitigation at successive stages of agenda-setting, formulation, and implementation. We synthesise this literature into a practical framework for making mitigation politically feasible, identify a set of persistent misconceptions that obstruct progress, and outline near-term actions that the evidence supports. The central challenge of mitigation is no longer identifying effective instruments, but making them politically feasible under real-world conditions.

title: Leveraging LLMs to assist tourists at destinations – The opportunities and risks of deploying open-source humanoid robots
authors: Yash Pandey, Spencer Kayser, Marius Portmann, Siamak Layeghy, Sara Dolnicar
abstract: LLMs are transforming tourist search behaviour. Tourists currently access LLMs on phones, tablets, and laptops. Open-source humanoid robots change this: the LLM becomes embodied and physically situated at the destination. This conceptual paper develops a framework for understanding the consequences of deploying open-source humanoid robots in tourism. The framework rests on two constructs. Embodied authority transfer describes how tourists reattribute LLM output from a private planning tool to the destination's official service infrastructure when delivered by a robot hosted in a tourism setting. Capability asymmetry describes the gap between what an embodied LLM can fluently discuss and what it can accurately know or actually do. The article discusses deployment scenarios and risk, and offers a detailed research agenda.

title: Corruption in Nepal's Local Governments: A Case Study of Institutional Weaknesses and Citizen Outcomes
abstract: This case study deals with corruption in public procurement at the local government level in Nepal. Nepal established 753 local governments with substantial responsibility for public spending, including procurement of goods, works and services, following the adoption of the Constitution in 2015. Mostly today, public spending is the responsibility of local governments, especially on capital investment in infrastructure, such as roads, schools, health facilities and water supply systems. But the speed of devolution of responsibilities has not been matched by adequate systems of transparency, accountability and integrity. This paper explores the nature and extent of corruption in local government procurement in Nepal, drawing on publicly available data from the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority, Transparency International, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and government audit reports. The analysis shows that procurement is a high-risk area for corruption at the local level. Corrupt practices are many and include bid-rigging, inflated costs, shoddy work, kickbacks, collusion among bidders, political interference with contract awards, etc. The data show that many local governments do not follow procurement rules well, publish limited information and have weak oversight. Audit reports frequently find irregularities in procurement by local government. The paper investigates factors leading to procurement corruption including weak institutional capacity, political interference, lack of transparency, limited oversight by citizens and poor enforcement. The report ends with recommendations for improving procurement integrity, including better procurement rules, more transparency, capacity building, stronger oversight, more citizen participation, and accountability enforcement.

title: Beyond Blame: School Violence, Youth Despair, and the Failure of Containment in Recent Philippine Shootings
abstract: Recent school-related shootings in the Philippines, especially the June 2026 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban and the August 2026 shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, generated public pressure to locate a single cause: a teacher, a game, a security failure, a disturbed child, a family failure. This paper argues that such explanations are emotionally understandable but causally insufficient. Drawing on incident reporting, official and reported-official statements, verified WHO Global School-based Student Health Survey data, DepEd Region VIII memoranda, public-health and threat-assessment literature, and C. G. Jung's Modern Man in Search of a Soul, the paper proposes a different representation: recent Philippine school violence should be understood as a failed ecology of containment. In this frame, adolescent grievance, despair, humiliation, or rupture become dangerous when they converge with firearm access, missed warning signs, weak disclosure pathways, digital scripts or grooming environments, livestream/notoriety affordances, and institutions that are not yet able to metabolize distress before it turns into public violence. The argument does not claim that Jungian "spiritual crisis" is a forensic motive. Rather, Jung helps name the meaning-layer of youth collapse: psychic pain, futurelessness, shame, and disconnection are real in their effects even when they cannot be reduced to one external cause. The paper concludes that prevention must move beyond blame toward containment: firearm accountability, threat assessment, confidential reporting, anti-bullying systems, psychosocial support, digital-platform safeguards, and living forms of youth meaning and belonging.

title: Staying Long Enough to Stop Seeing: Autoethnography, Long-Term Immersion, and Tourism Research
abstract: Autoethnographic tourism research has typically been based on discrete journeys or bounded periods of fieldwork, leaving the epistemological implications of long-term residential immersion comparatively underexamined. This article argues that sustained residence produces a distinctive form of knowledge grounded not simply in prolonged observation but in the transformation of perception over time. Drawing on more than a decade of living and working across Nanjing, Hangzhou, and Wenzhou, China, it proposes a three-stage framework of estrangement, normalisation, and critical re-estrangement. Initial unfamiliarity heightens attention; repeated exposure subsequently renders once-remarkable features ordinary and increasingly invisible; disciplined analytical attention can then return the researcher to these normalised environments with a capacity to recognise recurrence, pattern, and institutional continuity. Through examples of everyday urban landscapes and the seasonal infrastructure underlying Hangzhou's elevated-highway flower displays, the article demonstrates how long-term immersion makes visible processes that shorter encounters may register only as isolated events or spectacles. Critical re-estrangement therefore offers a methodological means of converting habituation from an apparent limitation of long-term residence into an analytical resource.

title: Detention as a disabling institution: Age-related health disparities in the US immigration detention system
abstract: From 2008 to 2018, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement apprehended over two million noncitizens in the US interior. However, data on detained immigrants' health is limited, with a particular lack of research on older detained immigrants, despite the distinct vulnerabilities aging individuals confront within and outside carceral settings. Immigrants face diverse structural challenges as they age, and incarcerated individuals experience accelerated aging and have worse health relative to non-incarcerated individuals, due to exposure to structural disadvantage, coupled with the health harms of incarceration itself. Using data from the Immigrant Detention Survey (n=495) and the National Health Interview Survey (n=8,383), and drawing on theories of aging in carceral settings, immigrant health and aging, and immigration policies as structural determinants of health, I address two critical and unresolved questions: What is the health profile of older detained adults, relative to younger adults? How do age-related health disparities among detained immigrants compare to those of non-detained immigrants? My findings reveal age-related health disparities in detained and non-detained populations. I also find much higher rates of poor health among detained immigrants than in the non-detained population, regardless of age. Results suggest immigration detention may be considered a mass disabling institution linked to poor health across the life course and may exacerbate age-related disparities, highlighting the need for more humane and equitable immigration and health policies.

title: A Foot in the Door: Ethnic Employment Quotas and Democratic Attitudes in Uruguay
abstract: Does bringing a marginalized group into the state raise its members' trust in democratic institutions? Uruguay's 2013 Ley 19.122, reserving eight percent of public-sector hires for Afro-descendant citizens, offers a rare test on the dimension representation theory names. Using the Uruguayan household survey and eight waves of the Latinobarómetro, we document a genuine but small first stage, Afro-Uruguayan public employment rose about 1.3 percentage points, a composition shift rather than a net gain, against a target the state met only fractionally. In addition, as second stage delivered a precise attitudinal null, with equivalence tests rejecting effects larger than roughly 0.15–0.20 standard deviations. The result establishes a scope condition rather than a refutation: at this level of exposure, bureaucratic inclusion produces no measurable attitudinal return. How much inclusion is required before the representation mechanism fires remains an open and newly quantifiable question.

title: The development of patriotism among youth in the EU
abstract: The article separates patriotism from nationalism and blind allegiance while examining the developmental trajectory of patriotism among young people in the European Union. Integrating identity status theory, social identity theory, and political socialization models, it constructs a developmental account of how patriotism matures from childhood through emerging adulthood. The review defines mature patriotism through four properties: differentiation, integration, criticality, and self-authorship. It identifies a shift from uncritical, affective attachment in childhood to a potential for “constructive patriotism”—characterized by critical loyalty and dual national-European identification—in later stages. Key mechanisms facilitating this maturation include open classroom climates, cross-border mobility programs like Erasmus, and digital engagement, though the article notes these opportunities are often stratified by class and education. Conversely, significant obstacles are analyzed, including populist mobilization, economic precarity, and East-West asymmetries in historical memory. The article concludes by proposing an integrative developmental-contextual model comprising three levels (substrate, elaboration, consolidation) and four moderating conditions. It argues that while a historically novel, reflexive form of patriotism is emerging among European youth, its full realization remains contingent on specific ecological conditions and faces ongoing threats from social stratification and political polarization.

title: Ambiguity-Robust Dictionaries using Contextualized Embeddings
abstract: Keyword dictionaries remain widely used in text analysis for their simplicity, transparency, and replicability. However, sensitivity to keyword selection and inability to account for context introduce measurement error that attenuates estimates and obscures real relationships. We introduce ambiguity-robust dictionaries, a text-as-data method that leverages contextual word embeddings to produce more precise measures while preserving the key advantages of dictionary approaches. Our method generates contextualized embeddings for all keyword instances, then applies constrained fuzzy clustering to determine the degree of each instance's membership in a target cluster defined by a small set of researcher-identified anchor words. This approach allows the construction of ambiguity-robust document level word counts, increasing precision and reducing sensitivity to keyword selection. We demonstrate the method using three applications: UN environmental discourse, ethnic bias in Kenyan judicial politics, and moral language in US Congressional speech. In each application, our method yields substantively more robust and precise estimates than conventional approaches.

title: Ageism by Default: Representational Ageism as an Upstream Risk in Medical AI
abstract: Age bias in medical AI is often treated as a performance problem, a perspective that fails to recognize an already existing risk: Generative systems may produce narrow, default representations of later life that enter health communication, patient personas, training materials, and care documentation. Because these representations potentially determine the needs, risks, and forms of support that take priority before clinical decisions are made, representational ageism should be addressed in bias audits, design documentation, procurement, and participatory review.

title: Generational Warfare Online? Social Media Use and Intergroup Attitudes in a National Survey
abstract: Content analyses document vitriolic generational discourse across social media platforms, yet surveys reveal moderate attitudes among the public. Does social media exposure create extreme generational attitudes? Using nationally representative survey data (n=1,221), this study examines whether total social media use and platform-specific usage patterns correlate with generational self-identification and intergroup attitudes among American adults. Results reveal limited associations with even frequent users not exhibiting greater generational antagonism. Platform-specific analyses reveal few significant effects, though YouTube use is associated with more favorable attitudes toward other generations. These largely null findings suggest extreme online discourse does not reflect typical users’ attitudes, implying that reasons for extreme discourse are connected to visibility mechanisms, such as algorithmic amplification and creators’ strategic performance. The study also demonstrates the risks of inferring population attitudes from content analysis.

title: The Social in International Relations: Mapping IR Theory through Social Theory
abstract: What conceptions of ‘the social’ underpin International Relations (IR) theories? Despite the growing engagement of IR scholarship with ‘the social’ dimensions of international politics, the concept remains surprisingly under-specified. Existing debates are theoretically rich but fragmented, offering limited guidance for understanding how different traditions conceptualise the social or how these assumptions are transmitted through the pedagogical accounts of the discipline encountered by students. This article argues that IR theories are underpinned by distinct yet often implicit conceptions of the social that function as unacknowledged ontological commitments. We develop a typology of six conceptions of the social grounded in social theory—functionalist, Marxist, rational choice, systems-theoretical, structuralist, and poststructuralist—and use it to re-read the traditions through which students most commonly encounter the discipline, from liberalism and neorealism to constructivism and critical approaches. We then trace how these conceptions have been reproduced and transformed through the discipline’s pedagogical canon taking widely assigned IR textbooks as our pedagogical point of departure. We show that the coexistence of heterogeneous conceptions renders the social both ubiquitous and under-specified, generating analytical and pedagogical ambiguities. By making these assumptions explicit, the article offers students, teachers, and scholars a clearer vocabulary for analysing, teaching, and debating IR theory.

title: The Fruits of Finitude: Reflexive Minimalism in Epistemology and Ethics
abstract: Reflexive Minimalism is a foundational paper proposing a minimal criterion for epistemic and normative stability: reflexive stability. A claim or norm is admissible only if it can survive its own application and does not undermine the conditions of reasoning, justification, or disagreement. The paper begins from epistemic finitude: finite agents cannot certify possession of final, unquestionable truth about ultimate reality. This does not imply relativism. Rather, it motivates reflexive humility: truth may be sought seriously, but no finite agent may treat their grasp of it as absolute possession. Applied to ethics, the framework rejects coercion grounded in uncertifiable ultimate claims and protects the shared space in which reasons can be given, challenged, and revised. This text serves as the programmatic foundation for a broader research project. A shorter core statement and further focused spin-offs will develop selected implications of the framework in epistemology, ethics, and related fields.

title: Agent-based Modeling and Simulations
abstract: Computational modeling and simulations have become increasingly relevant in the social sciences, offering powerful approaches for studying complex social phenomena. This chapter focuses on agent-based modeling (ABM) and its advantages for computational communication researchers, particularly for those who are just starting out. We introduce ABM, explain its core principles, and explore different types of models and their purposes. Through illustrative examples, we show how ABM has been and can be applied to address important research questions in communication science and related disciplines. The chapter then provides a practical step-by-step guide for conducting simulation research, outlining each step of the modeling cycle according to established methodological standards. We also highlight the importance of transparency and reproducibility through open science practices. Finally, we discuss emerging trends, such as the integration of large language models, which may shape the future of computational modeling and simulations in our field. This chapter aims to equip researchers, especially beginners in computational communication science, with a solid conceptual foundation and practical tools for incorporating ABM into their work.

title: Canvassing Mobilizes and Increases Vote Share: Evidence from a Local Election in Seattle
abstract: A long line of research has shown that door-to-door canvassing is a potent campaign tactic for increasing turnout and, in some cases, vote share. More recent work has theorized, however, that canvassing effects are largest in low-salience elections without party cues and concentrated among occasional voters canvassed closer to Election Day. In this research note, I test these theoretical expectations by examining the effect of canvassing in a February local election in Seattle for a housing-related ballot measure. Using a novel geo-coded dataset of seventy doorknocking campaigns over three months, I find that voters more proximate to canvassing operations were more likely to vote and that proximate precincts had a slightly higher vote share for the targeted ballot measure. Moreover, consistent with recent theorizing, I find that turnout effects were concentrated among targeted Democrats canvassed soon before the election.

title: The Quest for Peace in the Islamic Tradition
abstract: The Muslim world is one of the regions with the highest densities of conflict in the world (intra- and interstate). Yet it is one of the poorest ones in terms of conflict transformation resources both theoretical and practical. The foundational texts of the Islamic religion and the practices of the Prophet of Islam and the early Muslim community provide enough teachings to elaborate a comprehensive theory of conflict and peace. But the historical events the Muslim community went through and particularly the major political conflicts (the Big Fitna*) in the first decades of Islamic history prevented the emergence of a healthy approach to conflict. Today there is an increasing awareness for the need in the Muslim world to master the techniques of conflict analysis and transformation. This can be measured by the increasing number of young Muslims being trained in mediation or pursuing academic curricula in conflict transformation. The aim of this contribution from a Muslim author is to provide peace workers with a few resources from the Islamic tradition that can be used when addressing a conflict rooted in an Islamic context. Using the internal resources and a language understood by the conflicting parties has proven to be effective in conflict transformation. The concepts developed in the modern theory of conflict and peace may be expressed in words the parties are familiar with, and this is what this book aims to show. In chapter 1, ten basic Islamic concepts are briefly presented: dīn, islām, īmān, ihsān, rahma, haqq, karāma, ‘adl, jihād and sharī'a. These concepts are useful keys to understanding Islām; some of them are often misunderstood and misused. They will guide the discussions of the meaning of peace in the Islamic tradition. In chapters 2-4, the issues of peace and war, conflict and conflict transformation are addressed. In chapter 5, the value of work in the Islamic tradition and the requirements for decent work are then discussed, work conditions and environment being crucial for social justice and social peace. In chapter 6, the focus is put on the work of goodness, a concept that in the Islamic tradition goes beyond predication and humanitarian work and represents a holistic approach to human security. Chapter 7 addresses some issues related to Islam-West relations and the tensions that may arise between Muslims and Westerners, as well as the appropriate way to deal with them.

title: The Salafiscape in the wake of the ‘Arab spring’
abstract: This contribution aims to show that Salafi typologies are not static but change in time with the evolution of social and political contexts, and that no typology can fully grasp the complexity of the Salafi field. It proposes an alternative typology, based on how Salafis view and approach cultural, economic, political and military power, and gives a number of policy recommendations on how to deal constructively with Salafism.

title: Sufism, Politics and Violence: Reading Notes
abstract: This paper attempts to shed some light on the nexus “Sufism-Politics-Violence” and to show how Sufism, like other religious currents, spans a wide spectrum and how it would be misleading to consider Sufis’ approach to politics and violence in an indiscriminate way. The aim is to draw the attention of academics and policy makers to the fact that opposing Sufis to other Islamic currents such as the Muslim Brotherhood, the Salafis or the Tablighis is not the right way to prevent or counter extremism. On the contrary, such an approach is not only ineffective but may be counterproductive and prompt sectarian violence.

title: Addressing Violence and Extremism: The Importance of Terminology
abstract: The aim of this paper is to provide some elements that will hopefully contribute to a more accurate definition of the terms used in the context of extremism and violence, to attempt a descriptive model of the extremization process that encompasses the various paths leading to violence, and to discuss the various approaches to de-extremization. Contrary to the claim of some proponents of hard security approaches, explaining extremism and terrorism is not equivalent to justifying such phenomena. Understanding the process of extremization is a necessity for all those responsible for peace and security because it enables them to deal with it more effectively. Since “violent extremism” is often used to refer to Islamic contexts, which is in itself problematic, there will be some focus on the Islamic perspective in this paper.

title: Four Criteria for Differentiating Religious Entities
abstract: The attitude towards religion and an undifferentiated approach of religious currents result in many contexts in disastrous policies that cause undesired tensions in both Muslim and non-Muslim societies. This paper presents four criteria that help approaching religious currents in a differentiated way, considering their non-homogeneity and the wide diversity within them.

title: Uncovering the Hidden Magnitude of Within-Race/Ethnicity Skin Tone Inequality
authors: Luyin Zhang, Varsha Menon, Sam Trejo
abstract: Decades of research have linked skin tone to meaningful inequalities in health and social outcomes among individuals in the same self-identified racial/ethnic group. Yet efforts to document and understand within-race/ethnicity skin tone stratification have been hampered by a fundamental data problem: in most social surveys and biomedical databases, skin tone is either not collected or measured imprecisely using coarse categories based on a single observer’s judgment. In this study, we begin by conducting an online survey to quantify the reliability of existing interviewer-rated skin tone measures. Then, using elastic net regression, we build a genomic prediction model for skin tone among Black and Hispanic participants in the Add Health study, with the goal of improving the accuracy and availability of skin tone measurement in admixed populations. Finally, we use these DNA-based skin tone measures in two longitudinal studies to explore within-race/ethnicity skin tone inequality in contemporary America. Predicted skin tone yields substantially steeper gradients in socioeconomic status and racial classification, indicating that interviewer-rated measures meaningfully understate the degree of social stratification operating within racialized groups.
