Our results suggest that genetically derived skin tone predictions represent a promising new tool for advancing research on colorism – and, via the ancestry disequilibrium regression framework we introduce, a path toward identifying the causal effects of skin tone.

title: The Role of Advisers in Mediating Worldview Conflicts
abstract: Mediation as an assisted negotiation is a complex process involving the parties in conflict and a third party (the mediator/facilitator), as well as several “fourth parties” who can either be “constructive contributors” with a beneficial role, who help support and steer the process in a positive direction, promote understanding, and encourage open communication to help the parties reach a resolution, or “spoilers” with a harmful role, who obstruct, disrupt, or undermine the process, often creating conflict or preventing resolution. A good mediation process design is one that identifies from the outset all constructive contributors and harnesses their beneficial role, as well as all spoilers and neutralizes their potential harm. This contribution addresses the role of advisers in mediation processes and presents examples of the involvement of advisers in processes conducted by Cordoba Peace Institute – Geneva (CPI) over the last two decades in relation to worldview conflicts.

title: Waiting Spaces as Mental Health 'Gyms': A Research through Design Framework for the Situated Activation of Wellbeing Micropractices Where People, Time, and Infrastructure Converge
abstract: Cities have expanded access to physical wellbeing by placing exercise equipment in parks and public squares: infrastructure can offer opportunities for practice without requiring a gym, a fee, or deliberate search. This study asks whether a similar logic can extend to everyday mental wellbeing: can urban infrastructure facilitate voluntary activation of wellbeing micropractices where people, time, and urban infrastructure already converge, without additional time, financial cost, or specialized access? Using a Research through Design (RtD) approach, this study develops the Wellbeing Practices in Waiting Spaces (WPWS) framework through four phases: (1) qualitative clinical exploration using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (N = 8); (2) iterative design and urban prototyping in Amsterdam, Milan, and Barcelona; (3) exploration of everyday appropriation across seven countries (N = 41); and (4) comparative analysis of public-space wellbeing interventions. Low rates of voluntary flow interruption in high-flow contexts were treated as a generative finding, suggesting that instrumental movement may constrain attentional availability, leading the inquiry toward stationary contexts: waiting spaces. Three interdependent components of situated activation emerged: (1) spatio-temporal conditions shaping attentional availability (when); (2) inner human capacities, including mindfulness, appreciation, and compassion (what); and (3) visual mediating devices providing legible, brief, voluntary invitations to wellbeing micropractices (how). Across the urban prototypes, voluntary flow interruption, defined as stopping for ≥5 seconds, ranged from 1% to 5%. In Phase 3, 85.4% of participants reported mentally repeating the phrase, and 60.9% reported sharing it. WPWS is proposed as a transferable design architecture rather than a fixed intervention. It reconceptualizes waiting spaces as an underused spatio-temporal condition for situated activation, while recognizing that this proposition has not yet been empirically tested against other urban contexts. The findings do not establish causal or clinical effects, but provide a foundation for investigating how existing urban infrastructure can expand everyday access to wellbeing practices. Keywords: Urban wellbeing; Waiting spaces; Latent wellbeing infrastructure; Situated activation; Mental health equity; Trauma-informed design; Wellbeing micropractices.

title: Five lenses for co-creation across epistemic difference in transdisciplinary research
authors: Michelle Charette, Laura Levin, R. Shayna Rosenbaum, Caitlin R. Mullin, J. Douglas Crawford, Giuseppina D'Agostino, Sean Hillier, Gunnar Blohm
abstract: Co-creation has become an increasingly promiment approach to collaborative research in domains including health, education, sustainability, and design. Yet existing frameworks are designed for discipline-specific settings, offering limited guidance for research that spans heterogeneous epistemic traditions, institutional contexts, and value systems. This scoping review examines peer-reviewed articles to map dominant co-creation practices, rationales, and evaluation strategies. It reveals that most existing approaches are applied in relatively stable epistemic contexts, where problems, values, methods, and success criteria are well established. Drawing on science and technology studies and adjacent critical traditions, we argue that the central challenge of transdisciplinary co-creation is not simply expanding participation but negotiating epistemic plurality. Building on this diagnosis, we propose five complementary conceptual lenses (boundary objects, co-production, situated knowledge, critical institutional reflexivity, and multi-scalar evaluation) that together provide a theoretical and practical framework for organizing co-creation in transdisciplinary research settings. This framework reconceptualizes co-creation as an ongoing practice of negotiating problems, authority, evidence, and evaluation across heterogeneous systems of knowledge.

title: The Selective Politicization of Diversity Advertising
authors: Loureiro Lopes, A.I. (Ana Isabel), Alberto Lopez Ortega, Mariken van der Velden
abstract: Corporations increasingly feature minority families in mainstream advertising, positioning themselves as inclusive civic actors. Yet whether audiences read such representation as ordinary marketing or as a political statement—and whether all minorities are read alike—remains unclear. We field a pre-registered survey experiment in the Netherlands (N≈1,500), randomly exposing respondents to a supermarket advertisement depicting a control (white, heterosexual), Muslim, or same-sex family. Minority-family advertisements are perceived as substantially more political than the control and shift perceptions of the brand to the ideological left, both in abstract placement and in concrete party association. These effects are markedly selective: the Muslim-family advertisement is read as roughly twice as political as the same-sex advertisement, and is the only condition to lower purchase intention, and does so precisely through the perception that it is political. Issue attributions are domain-specific: the same-sex advertisement moves perceived brand support for LGBTQ+ rights, the Muslim advertisement perceived support for immigration—and, contrary to expectations, these reactions are broad rather than confined to right-wing consumers. The findings reveal a selective politicization of corporate inclusion, in which ethno-religious diversity is politicized and commercially penalized while sexual-orientation diversity is comparatively normalized.

title: Exposure to Homeless Shelters and Support for Policy Remedies
authors: Jacob Brown, Adrian C. Pietrzak, Alexander Sahn
abstract: American cities have rapidly built new homeless service facilities - shelters and supportive housing - over the last decade in response to rising homelessness. We study how voters react to these facilities once they are built and operational, leveraging a pair of statewide ballot propositions to fund new homeless services in California. We find that voters living closest to newly opened facilities became more supportive of spending on homelessness services compared to those living further away. We argue and show using survey data that new shelters increase the salience of homelessness in the minds of voters, driving positive policy feedback. We rule out the effects of positive changes in street conditions, improvements over existing land-uses, and financial self-interest as alternative mechanisms. Our findings suggest that voters can reward policy action and that NIMBY opposition may be more prospective than retrospective.

title: How Segregation Fuels the Far Right: Higher-Educated Social Relationships Buffer the Politically Radicalizing Effect of Economic Insecurity
authors: Jona de Jong, Tarek Jaziri Arjona
abstract: In recent decades, economic insecurity has driven some lower-educated voters to the far right, while others have not moved. We argue that segregation explains this variation: Higher-educated friends and relatives hold relatively progressive views and norms against the far right, preventing lower-educated citizens from politically translating economic insecurity into far-right support. Using existing panel data from the Netherlands and original data from the U.S. and Germany, we find that lower-educated individuals in higher-educated networks are much less likely to respond to economic insecurity by moving to the far right. Differential access to economic resources does not explain this effect. Rather, novel network modules and an experimental manipulation of network salience show that network education levels condition how individuals politicize insecurity. These findings show that others affect how we make political sense of change, and suggest that societal resilience against growing far-right appeal depends on the mutual integration of its citizens.

title: Infrastructural Mothering under Ukrainian Displacement
authors: Tamara Fedotiuk, Lisa Marzano, Emma V. Ward, Valentyna Voloshyna, Antonia Bifulco
abstract: This article examines how displaced Ukrainian mothers with children organise adaptation under ongoing war, institutional fragmentation and temporal uncertainty. Drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with internally displaced mothers in Ukraine and Ukrainian mothers displaced to the United Kingdom, alongside four focus groups with service providers, the study compares how two displacement regimes shape care work, service access and future planning. The findings show that mothers’ care-centred aspirations motivate infrastructural mothering: unpaid emotional, administrative, educational and relational labour through which they create conditions for children’s stabilisation. As mothers direct time, skills and resources towards children, their employment, language learning, psychosocial recovery, belonging and future-planning capabilities may become suspended. By conceptualising adaptation as relational and care-mediated, the study advances refugee integration scholarship, feminist care theory, and comparative forced migration research by demonstrating how distinct displacement regimes reorganise maternal labour and unevenly distribute adaptation opportunities within displaced families.

title: Black Feminist Social Work: Centering Black Women's Knowledge in Social Work Theory, Education, Research, Policy, and Practice
abstract: Social work acknowledges Black Feminist Thought as a framework and praxis, yet the profession has not established a social work framework that explicitly centers Black women’s epistemologies as foundational to education, theory, research, policy, and practice. Although social work maintains a historical commitment to social justice, person-in-environment, and human rights perspectives, dominant theories and knowledge systems continue to reflect Eurocentric assumptions regarding knowledge production and professional expertise. This article introduces Black Feminist Social Work (BFSW) as a conceptual framework that centers Black women’s individual and collective lived experiences, intellectual traditions, historical resistance, and knowledge to inform social work theory, education, research, policy, and practice. Drawing upon Black feminism, Black Feminist Thought, Womanism, Intersectionality, and the profession’s ethical commitments, the BFSW framework proposes a necessary shift from positioning Black women primarily as a population to be studied to recognizing them as producers of transformative knowledge. This article introduces four organizing principles, the Four C’s: Centering, Contextualizing, Co-Creating, and Changing, as foundational processes for Black Feminist Social Work and discusses the implications for curriculum development, clinical practice, research methodologies, policy advocacy, and future scholarship. Rather than positioning Black Feminist Social Work as an alternative specialization, this framework argues that centering Black women’s knowledge expands the social work profession’s capacity to pursue equity, liberation, and social transformation.

title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs? Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

title: Co-Writing the Self: Conversational AI as a Reflective Partner in Narrative Identity Reconstruction
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in writing and reflective practice, yet limited empirical research has examined how sustained interaction with conversational AI may mediate narrative identity. This study explores how ongoing engagement with ChatGPT shaped self-reflection, authorship, authenticity, and the interpretation of lived experience. Guided by an interpretivist paradigm, the study employed analytic autoethnography based on sustained interaction with ChatGPT across a purposively bounded longitudinal conversational corpus on academic, professional, and personal contexts. Conversational transcripts and reflective journal records were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Narrative Analysis, integrating Narrative Identity Theory and Post-Phenomenology. Analysis identified interconnected processes through which ChatGPT shifted from an information tool towards a reflective conversational partner, supported narrative integration, mediated reflection and decision-making, and prompted ongoing negotiation of authenticity and human authorship. ChatGPT contributed linguistic formulation, conceptual organisation, and alternative interpretive possibilities; however, experiential ownership, evaluative authority, and ethical responsibility remained with the researcher. The study develops the Human–AI Narrative Co-Construction Framework (HANCF) to conceptualise narrative reconstruction as a recursive process of AI-mediated reflection governed by human evaluative and narrative authority. The findings suggest that conversational AI may participate in narrative identity reconstruction without possessing narrative identity or displacing human authorship. The study contributes an autoethnographic account of sustained human–AI interaction and offers a framework for understanding how reflective partnership with conversational AI may extend human meaning-making while preserving experiential and ethical authority.

title: Social Stressors and Gender Inequalities in Post-COVID-19 Syndrome: Evidence from a Population-Based Cohort in Germany
authors: Nicolai Gröpler, Meike Dirks, Andrea Hildebrandt, Thomas Keil, Ann-Kathrin Knak, Sina M. Pütz, Mandy Roheger, Antje Wulff, Gundula Zoch
abstract: Women report post-COVID-19 symptoms more often and more severely than men, but the contribu-tion of socially structured stress exposure to this difference is largely unexamined. Social stressors are particularly relevant in the context of infectious diseases such as COVID-19, as they may influ-ence health outcomes through hormonal processes and their impact on immune function. This study examines whether stressors and coping resources in work and family life are associated with post-COVID-19 symptoms and whether they account for sex/gender differences in it. Integrating psycho-logical and sociological perspectives with contemporary medical knowledge, we hypothesized that social stressors influence the development of post-COVID-19 symptoms and, in part, explain sex and other socio-economic disparities. We utilized data from population-based COVIDOM study within the German National Pandemic Cohort Network (NAPKON-POP, 2020-23, N=2,941), recruited by local health authorities on the basis of a positive PCR test irrespective of symptom burden. 86 per-cent of women vs 76 of men reported at least one persistent symptom complex, with women report-ing a 4point higher Post-COVID Syndrome Score on the 0-59 scale. Results from stepwise linear regression models confirm statistically significant sex differences in symptom burden that mostly withstood adjustment for medical composition and social stressors. Accounting for perceived stress and resilience attenuated them by roughly one third, leaving a substantial and statistically significant residual gap between women and men. Overall, these findings suggest that sex differences in post-COVID-19 symptoms are bound up with differences in stress exposure and coping resources, and, thus, complement biological explanations.

title: Algorithmic Patriarchy: Artificial Intelligence, the Feminisation of Poverty, and the Limits of Governance
abstract: Nearly fifty years after Diana Pearce named the feminisation of poverty, the systems now deciding who gets hired, credited, or cared for were trained on the same discourse that has kept it in place. Patriarchal capitalist structures have long depended on women's unpaid labour while excluding women from the rewards of the economy they sustain. Neoliberal governance extended that arrangement, swapping a structural vocabulary of poverty for one of resilience, self-improvement, and personal responsibility. The neoliberal discourse brought the shrinking of the welfare state, and with it, a new vocabulary that spread from policy papers to self-help writing, human resources content, and coaching material. It has been produced at internet scale for four decades through the same text now training large language models (LLMs). Currently, this new vocabulary is embedded in the systems that screen résumés, and intertwined with the caseworkers who draft eligibility determinations. To understand algorithmic patriarchy and its relationship with the feminisation of poverty, this paper connects two bodies of scholarship: work on how neoliberal governance produces individualising discourse, and work on how AI systems inherit bias from training data. My contribution is to name and trace the mechanism by which patriarchy, neoliberalism, and unconscious bias combine to produce a vocabulary, reproduced by artificial intelligence systems, that may sustain the feminisation of poverty. Current governance frameworks audit outcomes but not the discourse producing them. This paper argues that language matters, and that identifying the unconscious bias it carries is a precondition for its measurement and correction – the basis on which governance bodies can design policies bypassing their own invisible limitations.

title: Guarantee Fulfillment, Asymmetry, and Desire Shutdown: Exploratory Multi-Level Evidence and Measurement Development for an Existential Guarantee System Theory
abstract: Terror Management Theory (TMT) holds that cultural worldviews buffer death anxiety by offering symbolic immortality and literal safety. But what happens when the worldview's promises fail to deliver? This paper introduces the Existential Guarantee System (EGS) theory, which proposes that societies function as guarantee systems: they promise rewards (stable income, status, family, housing) in exchange for participation, and threaten punishments (poverty, shame, exclusion) for exit. The Guarantee Fulfillment Rate (GFR) is the perceived rate at which these promises actually deliver. EGS predicts that when GFR declines, positive promise expectations decay first while negative sanction expectations persist — producing a Guarantee Asymmetry Index (GAI) that tracks the divergence, and downstream consequences including desire shutdown and post-goal disappointment. We present multi-level exploratory evidence for EGS across three measurement levels: (1) a preregistered pilot study (N = 68 after exclusion) developing a GFR/GAI scale with good internal consistency (GFR α = .94; desire-shutdown α = .84; sanction α = .88) and exploratory signals consistent with all five preregistered hypotheses, including a mechanical-overlap decomposition showing the asymmetry signal is direct (|r(GFR–S)| = .37 < |r(GFR–P)| = .78; composite GFR–GAI r = −.69); (2) an individual-level proxy test in a national probability sample (CGSS 2023, N = 11,326): opportunity-fairness beliefs predict ideal children count (β = .209, p < .0001) with the steepest slope in the youngest cohort (18–35: β = .306) — an age-gradient double confirmation (youngest cohorts hold the lowest fulfillment expectations and respond most strongly); (3) macro-level panel evidence (38 countries, 35 years): youth unemployment (an absolute-fulfillment proxy) predicts fertility decline (β = −.0099, p = .0012, two-way fixed effects), with relative-inequality proxies (Gini) showing the opposite direction — fulfillment failure is about absolute attainability, not relative distribution. All results are honestly graded: directional predictions matched expectations across all tests, but construct-level inference is limited to exploratory signals pending a fully powered preregistered study (N ≥ 300). The paper is positioned as the first empirical proof-of-concept and measurement-development wave for EGS — not as confirmatory validation. We discuss the Korea paradox (world-lowest fertility with low youth unemployment) as explained by housing costs (price-to-income ratio 24.4, top 12% globally), and the theoretical and practical implications for AI companionship as a novel guarantee system.

title: The AI Governance Execution Gap: Organizational Readiness as a Condition for Ethical AI Governance
abstract: Artificial intelligence governance frameworks increasingly specify accountability, human oversight, risk management, transparency, and lifecycle monitoring, but formal adoption does not establish that an organization can carry those commitments into consequential operational decisions. This conceptual paper argues that organizational readiness is a necessary condition for ethical AI governance. It defines the Governance Execution Gap as the distance between governance expectations and the institutional capacity to exercise decision authority, route risk, produce evidence, monitor deployed systems, and intervene when conditions change. Drawing on organizational readiness theory, the Technology-Organization-Environment framework, established AI governance standards and policy, and scholarship on translating AI ethics principles into practice, the paper develops an AI Governance Readiness Framework with five interdependent domains and corresponding Governance Execution Gates. It also introduces an Accountability Gap that distinguishes visibility, assigned responsibility, decision authority, and practical capacity to act. The central normative claim is that accountability and human oversight are ethically meaningful only when organizations can make those responsibilities executable under real operating conditions. A practitioner-oriented scorecard and illustrative cybersecurity triage scenario demonstrate how the model may support decisions without claims of empirical validation. The framework is proposed as a testable conceptual model for future empirical evaluation across high-consequence environments.

title: Sociotechnical Transition and Uncertainty in the Lithium Mining Industry: Technologies, Politics and Transparency
authors: Iván Ojeda-Pereira, Sebastián Herrera-León, Marcelo Lufin, Fernando Campos-Medina
abstract: Technological transitions in extractive industries are commonly assessed through technical and environmental performance, whilst their social and ethical dimensions receive little systematic attention. This article addresses that gap through the adoption of direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies in Chile, the world’s second largest lithium producer and the leading producer from salt flats. The National Lithium Strategy promotes these technologies as a response to social tensions over the use of water and brine in fragile ecosystems, and the conditions of their implementation remain open. Drawing on interdisciplinary work between the engineering sciences and the social sciences, we ask which technological and social uncertainties experts identify in this transition. Two expert workshops were held with 20 participants from industry, the State and academia, and their contributions were examined through inductive qualitative content analysis. The findings show five uncertainties: (i) there is no consensus on which technologies will be implemented or on the criteria for choosing them; (ii) the effects of brine reinjection lack conclusive evidence; (iii) the role and agency of the State remain undetermined; (iv) no mapping exists of the actors regarded as valid participants in the debate; and (v) there is no agreement on how the social sustainability of this change should be measured. We propose five public information infrastructures as a design response to these uncertainties, whilst acknowledging that transparency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ethical sociotechnical governance in the extractive industries of the Global South.

title: Inside the meat locker: anticipatory self-censorship and pressure on the vocabulary of American science
abstract: The U.S. federal grant terminations of 2025 have had a chilling effect on American science. Grantees whose awards have been renegotiated under threat of termination must now determine how the revised terms constrain the language they use when reporting their findings in peer-reviewed publications. Standing in the meat locker of anticipatory compliance, scientists face strong incentives to adopt conservative interpretations of what the revised terms require. In this commentary, I describe a case that surfaced during editorial review, in which an author excised disfavored terminology from a manuscript. Manuscript-level effects of this kind will ordinarily be invisible because pre-submission sanitization leaves no observable counterfactual in the published record. My concerns about the implications for the field are grounded in three recent episodes in U.S. history—the freeze on federal funding for gun violence research; the near-elimination and ongoing dismantling of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality; and the Toomey “hit list” of grants on HIV prevention and sexual behavior—each of which had durable adverse consequences for American science even without the backing of Stalinist repression. The post-Lysenko experience suggests that even if formal restrictions can be imposed and rescinded rapidly, the damage to human capital, training pipelines, and institutional trust may outlive the political conditions that produced them. Author-side strategies for lexical compliance (awkward periphrases, coded substitutions, and portfolio segregation) offer little defense against a determined state adversary. Their principal virtue is to make private accommodations visible as coordinated acts performed under duress—which is not nothing, because scientists deserve to have their compliance recorded accurately as compliance rather than as consent.

title: From Knowledge to Behaviour Change: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of the Tide Turners Plastic Challenge in India
abstract: Plastic pollution is a global environmental crisis which demands not only technological and policy responses but also changes in societal practices. The UN Environment Programme's Tide Turners Plastic Challenge (TTPC) addressed it by driving behaviour change through youth engagement. This mixed-methods evaluation study was conducted in India, comprised a pre–post randomised controlled trial in Delhi (n = 272) and Gujarat (n = 392), and 56 semi-structured interviews across six states, focused on the most engaged participants. TTPC participants outperformed the non-participants in personal responsibility (22%), problem recognition (23%), recycling knowledge (21%), peer environmental discussions (35%), and household recycling (55%). Qualitative results show that TTPC increased knowledge, fostered responsibility, and enabled youth-led adaptations to single-use plastics. However, structural barriers persisted, including inadequate waste infrastructure, limited digital access, economic constraints, and social exclusion. Voluntary behaviour change initiatives require a combination of motivational engagement and investment in enabling infrastructure to sustain impact.

title: The sociolinguistic labor of incarcerated people
authors: Gabriella Licata, Robert Tyler, Mesro Coles, Anthony Habib Watkins, Brian Asey Gonsoulin
abstract: Through participatory action research, we draw on interviews with 40 incarcerated students to examine how linguistic practices are shaped by institutional power in carceral environments. We argue that the magnitude of surveillance under incarceration produces sociolinguistic labor: the effortful management of one’s communicative repertoire. Our analysis identifies a distinctive form of dual-direction sociolinguistic labor, whereby incarcerated individuals are required to extend their repertoires both toward stigmatized vernaculars to gain social capital and toward hyperstandardized registers for institutional capital. We examine this dynamic across educational, social, and procedural domains, with particular attention to boardspeak—an emotionally-constrained, bureaucratic register through which rehabilitation is performed and assessed at a Board of Parole hearing. By situating these practices within broader critical linguistic theories and perspectives, we show incarcerated people self-surveil and create, prompting varying levels of sociolinguistic labor and innovation that are mediated by race, ethnicity, ability, socioeconomic class, and in-group membership. These findings demonstrate how high-stakes, surveilled environments intensify the stakes of language use and reshape the boundaries of communicative agency.

title: Blood-pressure reading and quality-control choices move India's raised-blood-pressure prevalence several times beyond its sampling error: an executable multiverse analysis of NFHS-4 and NFHS-5
abstract: Background. National estimates of raised blood pressure from the same survey microdata differ substantially across published analyses of India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS). NFHS measures blood pressure on a single occasion, so every estimate here concerns raised blood pressure on one measurement occasion, not clinically diagnosed hypertension. How much of the spread across published estimates is attributable to defensible analytical choices, rather than to sampling variation, has not been established. Methods. We encoded the analytical decisions of 20 published NFHS hypertension papers into an executable specification registry and ran 144 prospectively specified analyses (72 per round) on NFHS-4 and NFHS-5 person-recode microdata, crossing eligible population, blood-pressure reading-selection algorithm, quality-control scope, case definition and survey estimand. Estimates use a Taylor-linearized ratio estimator with sex-by-five-year-age post-stratification to household-roster targets, which corrects the differential blood-pressure coverage of the NFHS-4 male subsample. Two estimand families are reported separately rather than pooled. Results. Holding case definition, eligible population and estimand fixed, the five reading-selection and quality-control algorithms move prevalence by 1.58 to 3.07 percentage points, which is 4.5 to 19.6 times the design-based standard error of the estimate. Only 70 of 480 sibling estimates fall inside a given specification's own 95% confidence interval, and 66 of 120 specifications have confidence intervals containing no sibling at all. Within a fixed case definition, state rankings are reproducible: every within-definition bootstrap interval lies entirely above the across-definition interval in both rounds. Disparity directions are robust, with all 432 specification-by-gap combinations positive and 428 surviving Holm correction. On the specifications matching India's national NCD monitoring indicator, the reading-rule choice alone moves the monitored quantity by 46% of the reduction the 25% relative-reduction target demands. Conclusions. Reading-selection and quality-control choices, each individually defensible and each drawn from published practice, move an Indian national prevalence estimate several times beyond its reported precision. These are the fields least often reported: the blood-pressure validity thresholds are clearly reported by 3 to 4 of 20 papers, and no paper reports every field needed to reconstruct its own analysis. Levels should be reported as ranges over defensible specifications; rankings and disparity directions can be reported as point findings. Code, specification registry with per-field source quotes, and the full results archive are deposited.

title: The Best-Partner Paradox: Encounter Paths Strongly Determine Partner Identity but Only Moderately Affect Population-Level Relationship Welfare in an Agent-Based Model
abstract: Partner choice is commonly framed as a search for the uniquely ‘best’ person, yet romantic relationships emerge from sequential encounters, mutual acceptance, accumulated interaction, and exposure to unpredictable life events. We developed a theoretical agent-based model to distinguish two questions that are often conflated: how strongly encounter history determines who becomes partnered with whom, and how strongly it determines the resulting distribution of long-term relationship outcomes. Each simulated world contained 750 agents who searched over 20 rounds, evaluated five candidates per round, and formed relationships through mutual acceptance. Agents differed in excellence, relationship ability, and value position. Five choice strategies were compared: maximizing partner excellence, maximizing compatibility, balancing excellence and compatibility, satisficing, and random choice. Formed relationships accumulated dimensionless relationship capital over 30 simulated years through compatibility-dependent growth, relationship ability, stochastic favorable and adverse events, opportunity conversion, repair, and diminishing returns. Across 2,000 paired Monte Carlo worlds, maximizing compatibility produced the highest population welfare when singlehood was assigned a baseline value of 1.0. Its welfare exceeded excellence maximization by 0.0521 (95% bootstrap CI 0.0511–0.0530; paired Cohen’s d_z = 2.31), primarily because compatibility maximization generated a substantially higher pairing rate, although balanced choice produced the highest conditional mean relationship capital. Complete replacement of encounter schedules changed partner identity for 99.25% of agents paired in both simulations, close to the 99.73% independent-random-matching benchmark, yet changed mean relationship capital by only 11.45% on average and changed population welfare by less than 0.001. Mechanism ablation showed that repair after adverse events and compatibility-dependent growth were essential to welfare. A 15 × 15 robustness atlas found compatibility maximization optimal in 70.67% of 225 stochastic regimes, excellence maximization in 15.56%, and balanced choice in 13.78%, demonstrating that no strategy was universally optimal. Rankings stabilized well before 2,000 worlds. The model therefore identifies a best-partner paradox: the identity of one’s eventual partner can be highly contingent even when the attainable distribution of relationship outcomes is much less contingent. These results are theoretical consequences of the specified mechanisms and do not estimate real-world marriage probabilities or causal effects.

title: Cost of Safe Abortion Care in Kigali, Rwanda: A Retrospective Analysis of Hospital Billing Data
authors: Melina Gaju Uwamwezi, Stephanie Küng, Ritah Mukashyaka, Allan Higiro, Lawrence Rugema, Alain Favina, Aflodis Kagaba, Margaret Giorgio
abstract: Background: Rwanda has progressively liberalized its abortion law over the past decade, most recently through a 2024 order decentralizing safe abortion care (SAC) to health centres and clinics. However, the financial accessibility of legally provided SAC remains poorly understood; existing cost evidence in Rwanda focuses on post-abortion care, which has a different clinical and cost profile. This study assessed the direct facility-based costs of legally provided SAC in Kigali, Rwanda. Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of itemized hospital billing data from the Health Development Initiative (HDI) Rwanda for 236 SAC patients treated at 4 public and 1 private facility in Kigali from June 2022 to December 2024, including total costs and costs across 9 categories. Total and category-specific costs were compared by visit type using the Mann-Whitney U test; associations between characteristics and visit type were assessed using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. Results: The median total cost of a SAC visit was 62,353 RWF (range: 282-256,100 RWF). Consultation fees (94.9%) and commodities (92.8%) were incurred by nearly all patients, while medical acts (76.3%), imaging (75.4%), and laboratory tests (70.8%) were also common. Two-thirds of patients (66.1%) were treated as inpatients, with a mean length of stay of 3.1 days. Inpatients incurred more than twice the mean total cost of outpatients (96,572 RWF vs. 47,167 RWF; p<0.001), driven by significantly higher costs across most categories except examinations. Visit type varied by age group (p=0.014); adolescents (15-18 years) were least likely to be inpatients. Conclusions: Legally provided SAC in Kigali carries a non-trivial financial burden relative to household income, and heavy reliance on inpatient care, inconsistent with WHO guidance, inflates costs. These findings point to the need for a standardized SAC tariff, alignment of admission practices with evidence-based guidelines, and further research into drivers of cost variation in abortion care access.

title: the em—dash fails to em–erge: a registered null result for U+2014 in Polish and an exploratory function-word shift in 60,275 Sejm interpellations, 2015–2025
abstract: Since the release of ChatGPT (30 November 2022) a belief has spread that the em-dash "—" reveals text written with the help of a language model. This preregistered study tested that claim on 60,275 single-author written parliamentary questions (interpelacje) submitted to the Polish Sejm between 2015 and 2025. The decision rule was registered on OSF before the data were seen. The cue does not work in Polish. The registered hypothesis was not confirmed: in the decisive cell the share of documents containing an em-dash rose by 1.73 percentage points, but the confidence interval of that difference includes zero (−4.44 to +8.07 pp), so the second condition of the two-part decision rule was not satisfied, and three registered disconfirmation conditions fired. Follow-up tests point to the cause: models writing in Polish, and machine-translation flows, put a shorter dash there – the en-dash "–". The marker is anglocentric and is not suitable for Polish. An exploratory analysis measured something else: the frequency of Polish closed-class words (conjunctions, prepositions, particles) that a writer does not choose consciously. The reference point was an independently published corpus of Polish human-written and model-written texts, frozen together with its reading rule before measurement. From 2024 the distribution of these words moves toward the profile of the models (rank correlation rho = +0.368; 95% CI +0.228 to +0.461), while at a placebo date – the 2019 change of parliamentary term, where no such effect is expected – it does not move at all (−0.070; difference +0.438, +0.221 to +0.611). The shift survives four term-change controls. The change is small but widespread, and that is the correct description of its strength. Inside a single parliamentary office it is barely visible (median rho +0.125), yet it points the same way in 61 of 84 offices that could be measured separately (72.6%, one-sided p = 2·10⁻⁵), against 53.8% at the control date, which is what chance produces. There is no sudden jump at the date of the ChatGPT release. The change becomes visible in 2024 and unambiguous in 2025, and the shape of the transition (ramp versus late step) is not identified. The result describes a shift across a whole population of documents and allows no statement about the authorship of any single document or about any individual member of parliament. It does not establish a cause: changes in office staff, in subject matter and in editing practice remain possible explanations alongside tools. An independent reimplementation, with no access to the author's code, reproduced the corpus, the deduplication, the author panel and the headline analyses from raw HTML down.

title: CLAIM: Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging - A Theory of How Conversational AI Shapes Minority and Majority Voices in Group Deliberation
authors: Do Hoang Phuong Nhi, Suzanne van Gils, Christoph Lutz
abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes communicative spaces preceding social interaction, yet its effects are often studied in isolation from subsequent group dynamics. Recognizing this gap, we propose the Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging (CLAIM) theory, which argues that pre-deliberative AI interaction calibrates perceived opinion legitimacy and shapes voice in group deliberation. Drawing on AI sycophancy, the Spiral of Silence, and multi-level legitimacy literature, CLAIM proposes that high AI sycophancy increases validity and propriety beliefs, whereas opposition from AI deflates them. Moreover, structural opinion status moderates these effects: AI sycophancy can generate a compensatory voice effect for opinion-minority participants, while AI challenge can produce compounded silencing. Additionally, a legitimacy shock may emerge when minority-opinion holders encounter group compositions that contradict AI-calibrated legitimacy beliefs. Together, CLAIM extends AI sycophancy research by theorizing conversational AI as a legitimacy-calibrating force that can reshape voice in group deliberation, particularly under structural communicative inequality.

title: Locating the evidence: a Minimal Geography scale for the geographic locatability of research, demonstrated on LGBTQ+ fertility studies
authors: Boyana Buyuklieva, Hanxi Wang, Martin Gozzi
abstract: Background: Reporting checklists require a setting to be stated, but are satisfied at any granularity: "conducted in the United States" complies while remaining placeless. Access to fertility care and assisted reproduction depends heavily on where people live, and evidence-appraisal frameworks (GRADE indirectness, CERQual relevance) presuppose that a study's setting can be ascertained. Yet how practically locatable a study's evidence is (i.e., whether a reader can tell where it was produced) has rarely been treated as a measurable property. Methods: We introduce Minimal Geography (MG), a five-point ordinal scale rating how precisely a study's evidence can be resolved to a real place, from placeless (MG 1) to a named local site whose own population was sampled (MG 5), with a self-contained codebook. We applied it to 116 primary studies of LGBTQ+ fertility intentions identified through a scoping review, recording the verbatim source excerpt behind every rating. A second coder blind-rated a 10% sample. Results: Geographic locatability is strongly bimodal: 91 of 116 studies (78.4%) are vague (MG 1-2), two sit at the anonymised midpoint, and 23 (19.8%) are clearly locatable (MG 4-5). We observe the locatable minority to be concentrated in named specialist clinics, predominantly in the US. Quantitative studies were far more often locatable than qualitative ones, reflecting how each design recruits. Blind double-coding showed 75% band agreement and a linearly weighted kappa of 0.68. The instrument, codebook, and dataset are openly deposited (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21496412) to invite comparator corpora test of whether our observed bimodal distribution is distinctive or typical. Conclusions: Reporting compliance is not locatability and we discuss the coarsest-safe-level reporting (CSLR). We conclude that CSLR must state the most specific geography compatible with participant safety, and importantly, flag deliberate masking.

title: Detecting Coordinated Posting Behavior on Social Media. Introducing and Evaluating the Embedding-Based Tool ‘coorsim’
abstract: The detection of coordinated behavior on social media is an effective heuristic for uncovering organized manipulation of online publics. Existing detection tools rely on identifying identical or lexically similar content disseminated rapidly by networks of accounts. However, these tools are ill-suited to detect the coordinated posting of semantically similar content. This is a shortcoming in the age of LLMs that enable the large-scale generation of diverse yet semantically equivalent content. In this paper, we introduce and systematically evaluate coorsim, an open source R package for for detecting semantically similar coordinated posting. The package provides a platform-agnostic end-to-end workflow encompassing embedding retrieval, coordinated community detection, automated community labeling, and visualization. We systematically evaluate its performance against the most comprehensive benchmark dataset of known influence operations to date, covering 15 international campaigns. Across 3,780 evaluated parameter combinations, the best stable configuration achieved an overall F1 of 0.69. Using multilevel Bayesian regression models, we isolated the influence of parameter choices. We also provide a qualitative assessment of automatically generated community labels. Our results demonstrate that coorsim provides a valid, albeit not flawless, contribution to closing a gap in the landscape of computational tools for detecting coordinated online behavior.

title: Five Percent Re-runnable: An Audit of Disclosure in LLM-Based Social Science
abstract: We audited 133 arXiv papers from 2023–2026 (full text obtainable for 129), plus 38 DOAJ-listed open-access journal articles as a comparison group, checking seven disclosure fields in each. We define a study as re-runnable when three conditions hold together: it names a specific model snapshot, its prompt text is obtainable, and it provides code or data. Seven of 129 papers (5%) are re-runnable. Two figures stand out: 29% name a specific model snapshot, and 1 paper in 129 reports a random seed. The structural finding is that of the 21 papers whose prompt text is obtainable at all, about half (11) have it only in a code repository rather than in the paper. The journal group discloses less on six of seven fields, but n=38 is too small to separate that difference from sampling variation — we therefore read this as no evidence that peer review supplies the missing material, not as evidence that it makes disclosure worse.

title: Local Governance and Maternal Health Outcomes: A Case Study of Nepal’s Decentralized Health Reforms
abstract: Nepal has made impressive gains in reducing maternal deaths in the last 25 years. The maternal mortality ratio dropped from 539 to 151 deaths per 100,000 live births between 1996 and 2022. During the same period, skilled birth attendance rose from 9% to 77% and institutional delivery from 8% to 79%. Alongside these improvements have been major reforms in the health system, especially decentralization. The Local Self-Governance Act of 1999 assigned local bodies responsibility of health facilities. In 2015, the Constitution of Nepal established a federal system with 753 local governments responsible for basic health services. This case study explores the role of decentralization in improving maternal health outcomes in Nepal. It draws on data from national demographic and health surveys, policy documents and global health estimates. The study finds that decentralization was helpful as it increased local resources, improved community participation, strengthened accountability and supported national programs such as the Aama Program. However, the challenges remain and include inadequate local capacity, lack of clarity of roles, quality gaps and disparities between rich and poor, urban and rural and between provinces. Nepal’s experience provides important lessons for other countries looking to reduce maternal mortality rates through devolved health systems.

title: What Drives Legislative Anger? Multimodal Evidence from South Korea's National Assembly
abstract: Legislative anger is often understood as expressive representation, a signal that legislators passionately defend constituent interests. We argue that partisan blame underpins these displays, especially when parties attack one another over alleged misconduct. Using deep-learning models, we measure vocal and facial anger across 355 hours of plenary debate in South Korea's 20th National Assembly (2016-2020), covering 11,060 speech segments by 247 legislators. We find that anger peaks when legislators discuss scandal, at twice the level of policy debate. Moreover, a quasi-experiment around the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye shows that the same legislators become angrier in opposition and calmer in government. These findings challenge accounts that treat legislative anger primarily as constituency signaling and highlight how partisan blame and institutional position shape emotional expression in legislatures.

title: A New Approach of Applying the 360-Degree Method for Performance Assessment of Managerial Levels in Mega-Companies
abstract: Questionnaires play the most important role in scientific papers and workplaces. Considering various applications, questionnaires may be designed in different shapes and types. In any case, it is critical to have a questionnaire with appropriate content and a pleasing design. There has been a lot of study done on the validity and reliability of questionnaires used in performance assessments of managerial levels, but users are not sure whether their data is valid or not, yet (Before, it was observed that respondents used steady responses due to boring shapes of the options in questionnaire). This matter has a direct effect on projects or processes you are going to do. This paper considers a questionnaire using in performance assessment of managerial levels in a large company, and presents a new form of questionnaire which combines 5-point Likert scale with competencies definitions. New questionnaire is able to solve some problems in assessment of performance such as invalid data and low return rate. Cronbach's alpha (reliability of this questionnaire) using SPSS software is 0.891.

title: Housing and the False Promise of Abundance
authors: Sophie Bandarkar, Tahir de Noronha, Maximilian Buchholz
abstract: Following the publication of Klein and Thompson’s (2025) remarkably popular book, Abundance has emerged as the key diagnosis and remedy for America’s housing affordability challenges. The book’s central argument, along with allied academic work, is that deregulation will substantially increase housing supply and in turn meaningfully improve housing affordability. We argue this framework rests on inconclusive and contested empirical ground. First, a thorough literature review of relevant research demonstrates the links between deregulation, supply, and prices are much weaker and more complex than abundance advocates suggest. Second, returning to descriptive evidence shows that the basic facts which motivate the abundance argument are also contested. There is no incontrovertible evidence of a major supply shortage in the U.S. The abundance movement’s hyper fixation on housing supply and deregulation risks foreclosing possibilities for other targeted interventions that have a greater potential for remedying the affordability crisis.

title: From Division to Action? Mobilizing Women Through Gender Inequality Framing
abstract: Though American women face significant economic, political, and social inequality, it has been far more challenging to mobilize women around this inequality than some other groups. In this paper, I use a multi-method approach to causally examine how women respond to mobilization efforts from women's movements and organizations. First, in a survey experiment, I find that frames that raise awareness of gender inequality and emphasize the need to build on women's progress significantly influence women's participatory intentions and political attitudes. To examine effects among those who are already engaged around issues of inequality, I then conduct a field experiment with a women's political organization. Results from this study suggest more mixed effects of outreach about gender inequality and progress, with null effects on email engagement yet increases in donation behavior. This paper has important implications for academic research on political behavior and applied strategies to engage women in the context of recent social movements and elections.

title: Examining reasoning in process recording: An exploration of instructions in guiding students towards social work competencies
authors: Jemel P. Aguilar, Debra Crist, Huangshu Xu, Maria Mangiameli, Shirin Sultana
abstract: This article describes an exploratory study of a sample of process recording instructions from field manuals used by social work programs. Process recording in this study is conceptualized as a mechanism for assessing competency-based education, in which students, supervisors, and faculty members gain insight into students’ professional reasoning procedures, strengths, and weaknesses. Ideally, instructions should lead students to demonstrate reasoning aligned with social work competencies; supervisors would examine students’ reasoning, and field faculty members can assess field-seminar-level professional reasoning. Using logic models to analyze how the instructions work, we found considerable gaps in the logic of process recording instructions that do not align with the goals of competency-based education or social work’s emphasis on evidence-based practice. We found that undefined learning mechanisms, assumed integration, unstructured evaluation, and vague learning goals hampered the connection between process recording and competency-based education. We discuss the implications of these findings for social work’s emphasis on competency-based education, evidence-based practice, and professional reasoning, and we call for further research on process recording in social work education.

title: Deleting the call does not delete the evidence: a within-recording validity test for passive-acoustic whale-call detection benchmarks
abstract: Problem. Detection benchmarks in passive acoustic monitoring are built from temporally clustered events, so a period that contained an annotated call may differ from a period that never did in more than the call itself. Diagnostic. We delete the annotated call from a positive window, replace that interval with background from the same window, leave every other sample intact, and measure ablation AUC — P(call-removed positive scores above true negative). Null 0.5; higher means more shortcut. A splice control applies the identical operator to windows that never held a call. Findings. On the DCLDE 2013 right whale upcall benchmark the trained detector scores a same-recording ablation AUC of 0.635 [0.552, 0.710] — both arms from the same 15-minute source recording, 887-window negative pool — against the 0.5 no-shortcut null. The splice control sits at the null (0.483 [0.455, 0.510], 889-window frozen stimulus), so the cut is not the effect. Pooled values are larger and partly a between-recording contrast; they are reported beside the headline and never instead of it. Two spectrogram representations never trained on the task reproduce the within-recording separability under a fitted logistic readout (raw tile 0.688 [0.606, 0.772]; random projection 0.687 [0.598, 0.770]), so detectors inherit it rather than create it. It replicates across 30 SanctSound day-sites (same-day-site 0.566 [0.528, 0.604]). Five preregistered mechanisms — hard negatives, receptive field, context access, capacity, temporally matched negatives — were tested and all five failed: we report a measurement, not a mechanism. A preregistered second benchmark in a killer whale regime, its clustering precondition verified in advance, did not detect the effect: zero of four evaluable provider × species cells survive multiplicity correction on the same-recording-day estimand. Recommendation. Report ablation AUC beside average precision, and name its estimand. ---

title: AGIR: a theory-based framework to evaluate impacts of game-based interventions for sustainability transitions
authors: Sylvain Dernat, Clara Fiorio, Myriam Grillot, Gilles Martel, Médulline Terrier-Gesbert
abstract: Background: Game-based interventions (GBI) increasingly embed simulation games within broader transformation processes targeting sustainability challenges. However, evaluation frameworks remain predominantly session-centred and learning-oriented, offering limited insight into how in-game dynamics translate into real-world practice change. This gap is particularly critical for GBI seeking to influence behaviours, coordination mechanisms, and institutional trajectories over extended time horizons. Method: This article proposes a framework for Assessing Game-based Interventions in Real-world contexts (AGIR), a theory-based tool designed to assess multi-level change processes in GBI. Drawing on program evaluation theory, behavioural sciences, and simulation and gaming research, AGIR structures evaluation across six levels (L0–L5): from game design and in-session dynamics (L0–L1), through learning (L2) and behavioural change (L3), to practice change (L4) and transformative systemic impacts (L5). The framework explicitly models mechanisms, contextual factors, and temporal pathways linking intervention design to sustainability outcomes. Contribution: AGIR’s contribution is threefold: it reinforces theoretical foundations by explicitly connecting design choices with evaluation concepts; it provides a comprehensive reference point enabling comparison across contexts through standardised levels and hypothesised mechanisms; and it functions as a formative accompaniment tool supporting ex ante hypothesis formulation, in itinere adjustments, and ex post impact analysis. By shifting evaluation from end-point outcome measurement toward process-oriented understanding of contribution, AGIR addresses longstanding calls for rigorous yet practical frameworks adapted to complex, action-oriented interventions. Conclusion: The framework is designed for adaptability across intervention contexts while preserving theoretical coherence. Though resource-intensive, AGIR offers practitioners and researchers a structured approach to assess whether and how GBI contribute to sustainable change, fostering an evaluation culture essential for demonstrating the impact potential of simulation games.

title: Stakeholders’ perceptions of AI-assisted obstetric ultrasound in rural and urban Kenya: a qualitative study
abstract: Introduction: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools gain popularity in maternal healthcare, understanding community and health system perspectives is essential for inclusive and ethical implementation. This study explores stakeholder views on AI-supported ultrasound for pregnancy care in Kenya, that emphasized trust, equity, system readiness, and the importance of community engagement. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted in two Kenyan settings: Nairobi (urban) and Kilifi County (rural). Fifty-five semi-structured interviews and three focus group discussions were conducted with pregnant women, partners, healthcare providers, Sub-County Health Management Teams (SCHMTs), Community Health Promoters (CHPs), and community and religious leaders. Data were analyzed inductively using grounded theory principles. Results: The participants viewed AI with cautious optimism. While many welcomed its potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and access, concerns emerged around data privacy, informed consent, quality of care, and over-automation. Reliability or trust was linked to transparency, human oversight, and the use of local data. Participants highlighted structural challenges, including weak referral systems and staffing gaps, raising questions about the health system’s readiness to integrate AI. Fears of equity and “pilotitis”, short-lived projects without sustainability, were also expressed. Conclusion: Findings from this study suggest that AI implementation in maternal health may need to go beyond technology development and deployment. Developers and relevant stakeholders may need to consider co-designing with communities, alignment with health system realities, and the integration of ethical principles such as equity, accountability, and transparency.

title: Sovereign ESG and the Hydrological Constraint: Rethinking the Determinants of Water Stress
authors: Aneta Kargol-Wasiluk, Katarzyna Lewkowicz-Grzegorczyk, Carlo Drago, Alberto Costantiello, Angelo Leogrande
abstract: Water stress is read in the sustainability literature as either a physical or an institutional outcome, but the two readings have never been tested jointly within the sovereign ESG framework. This paper estimates the environmental, social and governance determinants of the freshwater withdrawal-to-availability ratio across up to 170 economies observed between 2002 and 2022, drawing on the World Bank Sovereign ESG Data Portal. Three equations share the same dependent variable and differ only in the pillar supplying the regressors. Each is developed along three tracks: panel econometrics, comprising pooled OLS, fixed and random effects, between and weighted least squares estimators and two-step difference and system GMM; a competition among six clustering algorithms assessed on eleven internal validity indices; and a competition among six supervised learners used to validate the specification rather than to forecast. Water stress proves overwhelmingly structural, with 99.1 per cent of its log variance lying between countries. The governance block explains 38 per cent of cross-sectional and 4 per cent of within-country variation. The level of institutional quality, measured as the first principal component of four Worldwide Governance Indicators and absorbing 91.9 per cent of their variance, is unrelated to water stress in every estimator; its composition is not, with accountability relative to state capacity carrying a coefficient of −1.10 between countries. The dominant predictor across all three tracks is the female-to-male labour force participation ratio, whose partial dependence reveals a discontinuity concentrated in a five-point interval. Under cross-validation with countries held out, no flexible learner outperforms ordinary least squares.

title: Designing Biodiversity Credit Schemes: Combining Implementation Scale and Certification Metrics for Farmers' Participation
authors: Kota MAMENO, Masayuki Sato, Yasushi Shoji, Takahiro KUBO
abstract: Biodiversity credit schemes have gained attention as a mechanism for mobilizing private finance for biodiversity conservation. As primary suppliers of biodiversity outcomes in agricultural landscapes, farmers’ willingness to participate is critical to the success of these schemes. However, little is known about farmers' preferences for biodiversity credit designs, particularly regarding metrics used to certify biodiversity outcomes and the spatial scales at which biodiversity credits are implemented. To our knowledge, this is the first study to provide empirical evidence on how certification metrics and implementation scales influence farmers' preferences for voluntary biodiversity credit schemes. A discrete choice experiment with a latent class model were applied to examine Japanese farmers' preferences for alternative biodiversity credit schemes. The results showed substantial heterogeneity in farmers' willingness to participate in biodiversity credit schemes, with approximately half of the farmers belonging to a participation-averse group. In both groups, implementation scale was the primary determinant of participation decisions. Farmers preferred individual farmland scale implementation over coordinated participation. Certification metric exerted limited influence on participation decisions, suggesting that ecosystem-based credits can be implemented without substantially reducing farmers' willingness to participate. Additional bonuses increased participation among farmers already willing to participate, but had little effect on initially reluctant farmers . Membership analysis indicated that willingness to participate was positively associated with biodiversity policy awareness, biodiversity-friendly farming practices, pro-biodiversity attitudes, and expectations of branding-related benefits. Expanding voluntary biodiversity credit markets, therefore, requires not only financial compensation but also information provision, demonstration projects, and communication of potential market benefits.

title: Exploring the relationship between Productivity and Healthcare Systems
abstract: The approach explored the relationship between the Productivity and healthcare systems, particularly applied to developing Countries. Main results show that, majority Countries in developing worlds, do not have particularly the strongest affirmation and capacity to create and generate a strong healthcare systems. The majority societies are stunk in developing. These Countries in particular, have for example, a high level of Inefficiency to allocate the public expenditure to the sector in particular. However, the study shows that countries with weak healthcare systems are, naturally, the countries that have a lower labour productivity. Furthermore, this evidence is particularly enough to help understand how for example most developing Countries do not intend the respective expenditure to guarantee high quality healthcare systems and to improve health to society in particular, on the other hand, the existence of a high level of budget in these countries increases the healthcare systems in general. Thus, many of these Countries, the lowest level of healthcare expenditure, show that these Countries are naturally incapable to drive social protection in particular. On the other hand, when this evidence is particularly characterized, the Country does not improve for example the economic performance. Furthermore, high quality institutions, mainly the political institutions for example, help naturally to increase the quality of healthcare systems in general.

title: The Competitiveness and WellFair: An approach of Angola Competitiveness Fail
abstract: Competitiveness can, in particular, be a powerful means of improving efficiency and the high quality of products on offer, which significantly drive the market and naturally ensure the greatest possible diversity of products available. On the other hand, some countries, such as Angola, and other developing countries, naturally exhibit a significant lack of a competitive environment; this is further evidenced, for example, by the weak business environment that exists. The weakness of the private sector further helps to explain this situation; for example, in Angola, the two most significant companies are state-owned enterprises, which naturally ensure high and significant sustainability for the Angolan economy as a whole. On the other hand, the strong presence of the informal economy contributes to the creation of a poor competitive environment. Certain fundamental conditions are naturally identified as other key factors contributing to this economic inefficiency, chiefly the lack of adequate economic infrastructure. In many key industries, there is naturally a high degree of concentration; for example, in the telecommunications sector, where Unitel holds the majority share of the market. This concentration, in particular, typically leads to a high level of inefficiency in the services provided. Other services, such as water supply and electricity distribution, naturally exhibit high levels of concentration within the economy; these concentrations are, in particular, reinforced by the nature of the companies involved, the majority of which are public enterprises. Thus, in general, the analysis shows that high levels of industry concentration reduce the diversity of key products on offer and contribute significantly to negative impacts on overall welfare. In Angola in particular, this evidence is strongly consistent with the lack of local production, as the majority of basic needs are met through imported goods. According to the evidence, the absence of a strong competitive environment leads the market towards the emergence of negative externalities.

title: HORMUZ STRAIT GEOPOLITICAL DISRUPTIONS AND PERSONAL FINANCIAL VULNERABILITY: A Case Study of Mid-Career Professionals in India's Private Higher Education Sector (2019-2024)
abstract: Geopolitical disruptions in critical maritime infrastructure create ripple effects throughout economies, affecting not just international trade but also individual household financial security. This study examines how the Hormuz Strait tensions (2019-2024) impacted personal financial management decisions among mid-career professionals (35-50 years old) employed in India's private university sector. Using mixed-methods research combining survey data (N=847 respondents across 23 private universities in India) and longitudinal financial records, we document that geopolitical uncertainty increased personal financial stress markers by 34-42%, with impacts concentrated among professionals with high exposure to import-dependent sectors, international travel, or savings in foreign currency. We identify three financial vulnerability channels: (1) increased cost-of-living pressures (rising inflation, higher education costs), (2) income volatility (uncertain salary increments, job insecurity), and (3) behavioral shifts (increased precautionary savings, risk-averse investment decisions, delayed major financial commitments). Heterogeneous effects are substantial: professionals in oil-sector-dependent cities experienced 56% higher financial stress; those with daughters in higher education abroad reported 27% greater concern about rupee depreciation. We propose targeted policy interventions including employer-provided geopolitical risk hedging, financial literacy programs emphasizing crisis management, and institutional mechanisms for salary stability during global shocks. This research bridges macroeconomic disruption literature with personal finance vulnerability, contributing to understanding of how global events transmit into household-level financial decision-making in emerging markets.

title: Application of Justice in Nepal: A Case Study of Rape Criminal Cases
abstract: Legally Nepal has come a long way in addressing sexual violence, but there is a huge gap between the law in the books and the justice in reality. Rape cases in Nepal are showing disturbing trend. There are strict laws in place, but victims often face apathy, delay and systemic roadblocks that deny them the justice they deserve. Studies show that 70 to 90 percent of sexual violence incidents go unreported, due to fear of stigma, retaliation and lack of faith in the justice system. This case study examines the application of justice in rape criminal cases in Nepal by analysing the legal framework, statistical trends, landmark cases, systemic challenges and voices of survivors who continue to fight for justice.

title: Recycling fabricated narratives about an early-career researcher is not a valid defence: a reply to Caruso et al.
abstract: Here, I respond to Caruso et al. regarding their recent paper defending the Sardinian blue zone. Despite the brevity of the work, the paper relies on an extensive set of straw-man arguments, falsehoods, and libels. These appear deployed as little more than a coping mechanism in the absence of arguments, and the errors and misrepresentations are tallied below. However, rather than restrict the reply to raising these issues, it seems appropriate to use this venue to highlight some of the far deeper problems with the blue zones concept as a scientific, social, and financial enterprise. That is, it seems worthwhile to address this paper on a few scientific failings first, and its many logical and ethical failures second.

title: Antidemocratic Policing in America: The Institutionalization of Historical Trauma
abstract: Countries have begun reforms to align their police forces with a democratic policing culture. Despite significant progress, the United States has failed to fulfill a key aspect of democratic governance: democratic policing. Consequently, the gap between law and departmental policy, and policing culture continues to widen. This study aims to contribute to Forde’s theory by applying the antidemocratic framework at the institutional level to describe policing practices that have received widespread attention by exploring police misconduct through a power lens of regressive strategies. The sample includes extant literature and data from exonerees. This study uses an innovative methodology grounded in the GQI and integrated with grounded theory analysis to answer the research question: How does Forde’s antidemocratic framework, rooted in historical trauma and political demoralization, manifest in contemporary police-civilian interactions? Forde’s antidemocratic concepts—nativism, social distinctions, misinformation, fear, dehumanization, and subjugation—frame this study. The framework underpins the understanding of antidemocratic policing and how micro-level disempowerment and macro-historical trauma (colonialism) converge in modern institutions. The primary finding is that antidemocratic practices are institutionalized. Future studies on democratic policing could inform the field and policymakers on whether misconduct, particularly excessive use of force, is a symptom of police demoralization.

title: Classification testing: A new framework for drawing qualitative conclusions from quantitative estimates
abstract: Social scientists rely on hypothesis testing to support their research conclusions, but the standard tests are designed for testing one hypothesis rather than adjudicating between rival possibilities. We develop a new framework, "classification testing", as an alternative. Instead of selecting one hypothesis to test, a researcher conducting a classification test decides what qualitative distinctions ("classes") are most substantively relevant; the test either assigns the estimand to a class with error control similar to that of a conventional hypothesis test, or declares the result inconclusive. We argue that classification testing is superior to current practice not just when the objective is to adjudicate between rival possibilities but also when there is one research hypothesis to be tested, because classification testing exposes that hypothesis to refutation. We illustrate the framework by applying it to a well-known media experiment and offer an R package to aid in implementation.

title: Authoritarian Lenses and the Dynamics of Exclusion: The Radical Right in Chile
authors: Lisa Zanotti, Fabian Villalobos-Machuca, Francisco Roldán Duque, Joaquín Valenzuela-Pastén, Sofía Cuadra
abstract: This chapter examines the Chilean radical right through conceptual lenses developed primarily in the European context, using the case to assess the limits of those categories beyond their region of origin. It advances two conceptual claims. First, drawing on Stenner (2005), it argues that authoritarianism is better understood not as an ideology on a par with nativism, but as an individual predisposition activated by perceived normative threat — a lens through which social change is interpreted rather than a fixed doctrine. Second, it argues that nativism, understood as the fusion of nationalism and xenophobia in defence of ethnic homogeneity, is too narrow for a region where migration flows involve culturally proximate populations, and that civic-cultural nationalism captures the Chilean case more accurately. The chapter traces the rise of José Antonio Kast and the Republican Party and the subsequent emergence of the Libertarian Party and Team Patriota, and shows how authoritarian predispositions combine with nationalist, anti-feminist and anti-communist frames to construct migrants, feminists, sexual minorities and leftist actors as outgroups.

title: Caring connections: A systematic review of health and wellbeing benefits of intergenerational farming activities
authors: Rosamund Harrington, Marissa Lindquist, Susan Darzins, Mark Trotter, Robin Drogemuller, Heidi Olsen, Gert-Jan Pepping, Suzanne Kuys
abstract: Abstract Background and Objectives: Intergenerational farming activities, including care of plants, animals, and surrounding environments, enable connection with nature and participating generations. This systematic review aimed to determine health and wellbeing impacts of intergenerational farming activities for older adults, children/youth and community; key factors contributing to establishment, engagement in, and sustainability of intergenerational farming programs: and whether they support ‘ageing-in-place'. Research Design and Methods: A systematic search was undertaken of five databases. Studies could be qualitative and/or quantitative, involve an intergenerational activity/program inclusive of older adults and children/youth, report health and wellbeing outcomes and be written in English. Adopting a social ecological lens, qualitative data were synthesised and reported thematically. Quantitative data were descriptively presented. Results: Twenty-two studies were included. Seven themes relating to health and wellbeing impacts were identified: physical health benefits, psychological benefits, positive relationships and interpersonal skills, community and belonging, purposeful work or learning, environmental engagement, and connection to culture. Factors impacting establishment, engagement in, and sustainability of activities included planning and implementation considerations, partnerships, agency and anticipated future opportunities/benefits.
