No studies reported if, or how, intergenerational farming activities support ‘ageing-in-place’. Discussion and Implications: Intergenerational farming activities appear to offer holistic health and wellbeing benefits, reflecting Indigenous approaches to healing through connections to land, culture, and community. Establishing sustainable programs requires planning, training and partnerships. More robust research utilising objective measures is required to support findings. Further investigation is needed. Furthermore, studies investigating how intergenerational farming supports ‘ageing-in-place’ is recommended.

title: Older adults without a partner and adult children in Finland
authors: INVEST Flagship, alyona artamonova, Mirkka Danielsbacka
abstract: Background: Core-kinless older adults, i.e., those lacking a partner and children, represent a potentially vulnerable group. However, the whole population-level research devoted to this group remains scarce. Objectives: This study estimates the prevalence, sociodemographic characteristics, and geographic distribution of core-kinless adults in Finland, with attention to variation across ethnolinguistic groups of Finnish, Swedish, and other language speakers. Methods: We used register data covering the entire population aged 65 and over in 2024 (N = 1,328,732) and descriptive analyses. Core-kinlessness was defined as the absence of both a registered co-residing partner and any living children registered in Finland. Results: In total, 11.6% of older adults in Finland were core-kinless. Prevalence was 11.3% among Finnish-speaking, 10.3% among Swedish-speaking, and 30.5% among other language-speaking individuals. Migration background in general, being male among Finnish-speaking as well as being female, being older and having lower education among other language-speaking individuals are the characteristics of this group. The positive associations between municipal core-kinlessness and i) demographic dependency ratio, ii) the mortality rate among older adults and iii) the rate of home care clients confirm that municipalities where these older adults are concentrated also face greater demographic and service pressures. Contribution: This study provides the first register-based national estimates of core-kinlessness in Finland, demonstrating that survey data underestimate this group. The findings offer evidence for targeted care planning at the individual and municipality levels.

title: Does Democratic and Economic Benchmarking Matter for Affective Polarization? A Survey Experiment in Poland
abstract: This article examines whether international benchmarking, cross-national comparisons of a country’s democratic or economic performance, intensifies affective polarization among citizens. While prior research has shown that international economic comparisons shape electoral behavior, little is known about how such external evaluations influence emotional hostility between partisan groups. Drawing on a survey experiment conducted as part of the 2023 Polish National Election Study, the study tests whether exposure to negative international assessments increases affective polarization. The results reveal a striking asymmetry. Exposure to democratic benchmarking, information signaling Poland’s decline on democratic indicators relative to regional peers, significantly increases affective polarization, whereas economic benchmarking produces no comparable effect. These effects are conditional. Democratic benchmarking polarizes primarily among citizens with negative evaluations of the outgoing government, while leaving strong government supporters unaffected. The findings suggest that benchmarking is most polarizing when it concerns identity-relevant and normatively charged domains in which responsibility can be credibly attributed to domestic political actors. Overall, the study shows that international reputational cues can deepen partisan divides, reinforcing emotional boundaries between political camps rather than fostering a common ground for evaluating national performance.

title: Exploitation-based social class, class consciousness and political participation
authors: Agata A. Troost, Jaap Nieuwenhuis, Jonathan J.B. Mijs
abstract: Departing from recent discussions about social class and relational inequality, we investigate the idea of the power antagonism between the workers and capitalists, and the implications of this antagonism for political participation. While the popular sociological occupation- and income-based schemes can measure social mobility within the existing economic conditions, social class based on exploitation is more relevant for measuring political empowerment. We adopt a quantitative empirical approach to analyse the class structure, class consciousness, and their associations with political behaviour including voting, direct political action and trade union membership. We recreate E.O. Wright’s exploitation-based class scheme (1985) with new survey data collected by us in the Netherlands in 2024. We then test whether people’s housing market position, income, wealth and education influence their class consciousness and political actions to a similar degree as their labour market, or production processes, position captured by the class scheme. Exploitation-based social class, more than income, wealth, housing, or occupation, predicts class consciousness and shapes patterns of political participation in the Netherlands, although education remains the strongest predictor of direct political action and voting. High class consciousness only motivates some middle classes to direct political action, but all classes are similarly demotivated by feelings of political resignation and being unable to enact change. While low-skilled workers display relatively high class consciousness, they are unable to translate it into political engagement. Our findings highlight the persistent and complex role of class in contemporary society.

title: A National Portrait of Life Course Marital and Cohabiting History
abstract: Objectives Partnership histories encompass the duration, timing, and sequence of marital and cohabiting relationships that accumulate across the life course. Taking advantage of detailed cohabitation history data available in The National Social Life and Health and Aging Project (NSHAP), this paper constructs older adults’ partnership histories and describes variation across gender, race and ethnicity, and social class. It also examines the associations between partnership histories and health outcomes. Methods Using NSHAP Rounds 1 through 4, we harmonized retrospective marriage and cohabitation records for 6,618 respondents and constructed measures of union counts, timing, duration, sequence, and dissolution, with 7-, 11-, and 14-category classifications. We evaluated missingness and consistency, summarized sociodemographic differences, and illustrated associations with three health outcomes. Results Older adults married to their first spouse (37.7%) and widowed (14.9%) comprise over half of the sample. Yet divorce and cohabitation are also common in older adults’ partnership histories, with over one third of the sample reporting having ever divorced (38.5%) and having ever cohabited before a marriage (36.7%). Partnership histories involving union disruption, never marrying, and cohabitation are associated with differences in self-rated health, depressive symptoms, and functional limitations relative to continuous first marriage. Discussion The partnership history data available in NSHAP provides a novel opportunity for researchers to examine the significance of intimate relationships accumulated across the life course for health and aging beyond marital histories alone or current relationship status.

title: Incarceration and Deservingness: Experimental Evidence on Less Eligibility
authors: Christopher Berk, Lucas Nunez, Brett Burkhardt
abstract: A substantial literature on welfare politics shows that public support for redistribution depends on markers like need, effort, and reciprocity that sort recipients into deserving and undeserving categories. We test whether incarceration status functions as a particularly powerful deservingness marker, structured by the eighteenth-century principle of "less eligibility": that no one subject to punishment should fare better than the poorest free person. Using a pre-registered conjoint experiment with a representative U.S. sample (N = 1,929), we find that incarcerated applicants to an identical rehabilitative program receive substantially less public support than otherwise-comparable poor or welfare-dependent applicants — a penalty that persists even when the incarcerated applicant is shown to benefit more from the program than the comparison case. Decomposing the moral-cultural mechanisms behind this penalty, we find community-belonging and cost-benefit evidence each narrow it somewhat, while signals of the applicant's hard work and reliability paradoxically widen it. The incarceration penalty, we argue, operates as a durable boundary of moral exclusion rather than a correctable informational gap, with implications for how welfare-state and punishment scholarship jointly understand deservingness.

title: The Q18 Survey: Initial Validation of an Employee-Reported Outcomes
abstract: Employee surveys commonly assess individual attitudes and experiences, but fewer instruments integrate these with employees’ perceptions of organisational functioning. This study reports the initial validation of the Q18, a brief employee-reported outcomes instrument designed for employee listening, aggregate-level human resource and managerial monitoring, and perceived organisational assessment. A validation study was conducted with 3,350 employees working in France. Analyses examined score distributions, reliability, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) structure, discriminant validity, multi-group invariance, multicollinearity, and practical and nomological anchoring with the employee Net Promoter Score (eNPS). CFA model comparisons supported a correlated eight-factor structure comprising four individual outcomes and four perceived organisational outcomes. Reliability estimates were compatible with aggregate-level interpretation for human resource and managerial tracking, and invariance analyses supported measurement stability across the main segmentation variables. Q18 scores increased progressively across eNPS detractors, passives, and promoters. Discriminant validity received partial support: the dimensions were empirically distinguishable, but some remained strongly interdependent. By bringing together individual outcomes and perceived organisational outcomes, the Q18 provides an integrated interpretation of tensions or alignments between employee experience and perceived collective functioning and helps extend employee listening practices beyond the measurement of individual attitudes alone. Further research is needed to establish its longitudinal, organisational-level, and cross-cultural validity.

title: Using Geospatial modeling to Understand Spatial Job Access for TANF Recipients
authors: Gabriel Appiah, Arthi Rao, Latrice Rollins, Andrew Cooper, Alex Camardelle
abstract: Access to employment is central to the effectiveness of the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program, yet job opportunities are unevenly distributed across space. This study examines county-level patterns in job accessibility for TANF recipients, with a particular focus on African American (AA) populations and urban–rural differences in commuting behavior. Using data from Alabama, Louisiana, Georgia, Virginia, and the District of Columbia, we construct gravity-based job accessibility indices for high-, median-, and low-paying employment. Distance-decay parameters are empirically estimated from Longitudinal Employer–Household Dynamics (LEHD) commuting flows, allowing travel sensitivity to vary between urban and rural areas. Accessibility measures are computed for total employment and compared across AA TANF - majority and minority counties. We then apply hierarchical clustering to county-level indicators of accessibility, socioeconomic vulnerability, housing and mobility constraints, and TANF caseload composition. The resulting seven-cluster typology reveals distinct TANF opportunity contexts, including counties characterized by severe spatial isolation and others where high accessibility coexists with persistent disadvantage. These findings highlight the limitations of uniform TANF work requirements and support the need for place-sensitive, equity-oriented welfare policy design.

title: Strategic behaviour in decision support systems: a conceptual framework for observation in multi-stakeholder decision-making processes
authors: Monique Arkesteijn, Adinda Jongkind, Fatemeh Hedieh Arfa, Haiko van der Voort
abstract: While DSS are designed to enhance transparency and provide structure in complex, multi-stakeholder settings, they also influence actions of participating stakeholders and thereby their strategic choices. This paper reviews the literature on SB and DSS, identifies diverse forms of strategic action, and proposes a five-step framework for systematically observing SB in DSS-supported processes and environments. The framework integrates contextual dynamics, stakeholder motivations, strategic approaches, and resource use, offering a structured and comprehensive lens for analysis. By focusing on how stakeholders engage strategically in practice, rather than prescribing how they should behave, the framework enables a nuanced and realistic understanding of stakeholder interaction, behaviour, and power in participatory settings. This conceptual contribution advances both academic and applied discussions by providing a tool that supports empirical investigation as well as the design and use of DSS in real-world decision-making contexts.

title: Elite-Public Gaps on Salient Foreign Policy Issues: Experimental Evidence from the 2022/23 US Sanctions on Russia
authors: Anton Peez, Felix Bethke, Felix Bethke
abstract: Do citizens and political elites in Western democracies hold different views on foreign policy? ‘Elite-public gaps’ raise questions about whether elites represent public preferences and how much discretion they exercise. Research suggests that although gaps exist, they are significantly driven by ‘mundane’ compositional differences. We examine these gaps during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. We ran a paired experiment with US executive staffers (n = 253) and the US public (n = 1,002), asking whether respondents support increasing sanctions on Russia. We randomize information on real public polling highly supportive of sanctions. The public was less supportive than executive staffers at baseline, but more responsive to public opinion. Gaps shrink after accounting for basic sociodemographics. This extends research on elite-public gaps to cover salient real-world events.

title: Value-Based Adaptive Reuse: Design and Initial Testing of a Serious-Game Prototype
abstract: Adaptive reuse of heritage buildings requires stakeholders, and more specifically, architects to navigate interdependent questions of heritage significance, contemporary function, environmental performance, community benefit, financial feasibility, and approval of other stakeholders (developers, investors, and regulators). Process models can structure these questions, yet conventional validation methods reveal only part of how practitioners move between them under constraint. This paper presents the design and pilot testing of Architect's Design Challenge, a tabletop serious-game prototype developed to explore professional decision-making in adaptive reuse and to examine the practical legibility of the Effective Adaptive Reuse of Heritage Buildings (EARHB) process model. Players progress through six stations, allocate limited resources, select action cards, respond to stakeholder requirements, and construct a design proposition using four predefined project-value categories represented by coloured components. Two formative test rounds, involving students and architects, were organised around introduction, gameplay, and debriefing. The tests indicated that the prototype could stimulate explicit discussion of priorities, sequencing, resource allocation, and trade-offs. They also revealed a central design tension: abstraction supported strategic play but sometimes weakened correspondence with professional practice, particularly for expert players. The study contributes a transparent mapping between research constructs and game mechanics, identifies requirements for future validation, and shows how serious gaming could make selected moments of value recognition, translation into design choices, negotiation, and revision observable within a simulated decision pathway. The evidence is exploratory. It does not establish learning effects, behavioural validity, or transfer to real projects.

title: Understanding children’s housing in Australia: a data framework
authors: Amy Clair, Emma Baker, Lynne Giles, Claire Morey, Megan Robinson
abstract: This project examines the available data on children’s housing and wellbeing and current policy in Australia to highlight how housing affects children’s health and development. It provides policymakers with a guide to the different housing situations children face, identifies significant knowledge gaps and related risks, and proposes priorities for policy-relevant data collection and evidence development. The impacts of Australia’s housing crisis on children have received less attention than for other population groups. Accessible data collections rarely focus on them. Yet households with children are particularly affected by poor quality and insecure housing, and children’s physical vulnerability and dependence on caregivers increases the related risks to their wellbeing. This underscores the need for stronger data insights to support earlier intervention, better targeting and more accountable policy for children.

title: Toward an Intersectional Occupational Health Framework: Psychosocial Conditions as Allocated Exposures
abstract: Occupational health research treats psychosocial working conditions either as features of a job or as traits that help workers cope. This article proposes the Intersectional Occupational Health (IOH) framework, which instead treats these conditions as exposures that labor regimes allocate to differently positioned workers. Drawing on vulnerability theory and the sociology of work, the framework argues that a worker's psychosocial profile records where that worker has been placed, since who meets high-strain conditions, and for how long, is set by law, immigration rules, and welfare systems. On this reading, the uneven spread of these conditions measures a process that produces vulnerability rather than a tally of how well workers cope. The framework follows the path from social position to health outcome, and it treats a sound intervention as one that redistributes exposure rather than one that raises the average. Two cases, domestic work in Southern Europe and platform delivery in Germany, ground a set of recommendations for governments, ranging from household labor inspection to an enforceable presumption of employment.

title: Relay cooperation between women and girls during foraging trips among BaYaka hunter-gatherers in the Republic of the Congo
abstract: Children in small-scale societies contribute to subsistence and infant care from an early age, developing relevant skills through everyday participation. To examine how such participation is organised in practice, we focus on women’s daily foraging among BaYaka hunter-gatherers in the Congolese rainforest, where children frequently accompany adults. Using focal follows, we recorded mothers’ activity states - foraging, travelling, and resting - alongside helping behaviours of group members, including childcare, foraging, and basket carrying. We find that childcare, subsistence, and load-carrying responsibilities are dynamically redistributed through relay cooperation between women and girls, who are not necessarily kin. Infant care is frequently transferred from women to girls, enabling mothers to continue foraging without carrying infants. When mothers pause to rest or breastfeed, girls temporarily take over foraging tasks. These role shifts occur repeatedly within trips, revealing a structured yet flexible system that allows mothers to manage the energetic and mobility constraints of childcare while maintaining productivity. At the same time, relay cooperation provides girls with repeated opportunities to engage in both caregiving and subsistence, supporting learning through participation with women other than their own mothers. These findings provide insight into how children develop as cooperative actors through active participation in women’s subsistence and caregiving activities.

title: From humanitarian design to design for social innovation: a comparative experiment activating reflexivity on coloniality and power dynamics.
authors: Riccardo Torta, Marco Andrea Finardi, Abigail Turinayo, Victor Muwonge Semaganda, Marco Gobetti
abstract: This meta-research originates from two experiences of the first two authors, who respectively worked on a Humanitarian Design (HD) project in Uganda with Design Without Borders and on a Design for Social Innovation (DSI) project in Italy with Polimi DESIS Lab. Similar tensions emerged from both contexts regarding the relationship between the design teams and the communities engaged, highlighting the risk of perpetuating systemic oppression and epistemic injustice. To explore these imbalances, the teams were engaged in two sets of sessions, activating reflexivity on social structures embedded in their practices, to uncover potential dynamics rooted in coloniality and power. Where the Ugandan HD project served as a testbed for the approach and three reflexive tools, the sessions within the Italian project confirmed the initial proposition, showing the potentially broad impact of the application of reflexivity on oppressive dynamics within DSI projects. This experiment uncovered the risks entailed by engaging with local communities, raised issues about urbanity and rurality, different forms of knowledge and models of development, challenging the conception of modernity and recognising these foundational elements of coloniality even in a European context. Considering the exploratory nature of this research, the intent is to provide grounding for future critical inquiries within the wider DSI community, demonstrating the need to rethink current design practices from a liberatory and relational perspective.

title: Occupational AI Exposure and the Reconfiguration of Class Inequalities in Perceived Job Insecurity
authors: Daniela Bellani, Honorata Bogusz, samuel plach
abstract: Research on AI and inequality has focused primarily on employment, wages, productivity, and task displacement, while less is known about how occupational AI exposure is associated with workers’ subjective insecurity and how these concerns are distributed across social classes. This study examines perceived job insecurity among employed workers in Europe, distinguishing quantitative insecurity - fear of job loss - from qualitative insecurity - fear of an undesirable change in the work situation. We use the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey, linked to an occupation-level measure of potential AI exposure, to examine whether the class pattern of AI-related insecurity mirrors the conventional class gradient in perceived job insecurity. Manual workers report the highest average fear of job loss, but the positive association between occupational AI exposure and job-loss fear is concentrated among higher- and lower-grade service workers and is weak or absent among manual workers. By contrast, occupational AI exposure shows a positive association with fear of undesirable job change, but this outcome displays no recurrent class pattern. Exploratory analyses show that the service-class association with job-loss fear is especially visible among tertiary-educated and older workers and among those who do not report using AI directly at work, while cross-national estimates indicate that the pattern appears across several institutional contexts. The findings suggest that occupational AI exposure may reconfigure rather than sim-ply reproduce existing inequalities in insecurity, as the workers reporting the highest baseline insecurity are not those among whom the association with AI exposure is most pronounced

title: Knowledge to action in alternative crisis response: Examining alignment and misalignment between evidence and practice
authors: Megan Wheeler Rowe, Claire Ryder, Amanda Mathew, Jenny Hui, Brandon Barksdale, Leyna Lowe, Andrew David Eaton
abstract: Background: Alternative crisis response models have rapidly emerged to reorganize mental health crisis care away from traditional police-led responses. It is important to explore whether the existing evidence base on co-response and civilian-led models aligns with the perspectives of those closest to the field. Aims: This study examined points of alignment and misalignment between synthesized evidence from two scoping reviews and the lived, practice-based, and systems-level knowledge of key informants in alternative crisis response. Methods: From August-December 2025, 33 crisis response key informants in Canada and the United States participated in semi-structured interviews prompted by the scoping reviews. Data were analyzed using directed qualitative content analysis, with 13 sensitizing domains regarding key processes of co-response and civilian-led models. Results. Participants strongly aligned with reducing police involvement and developing distinct crisis response teams. Misalignment most often appeared as contextualization or extension, especially around police involvement, interprofessional collaboration, team composition, local service capacity, and public narratives. Domains related to monitoring, evaluation, and model variation had high counts of no available data. Conclusions: Findings suggest that evidence on alternative crisis response is broadly resonant but requires contextualization to reflect the realities of practice and the sustainability needs of a rapidly evolving field.

title: Spirit Becoming Matter: A Thematic Analysis of Creation Stories
abstract: Objective This qualitative study examined the creation stories from a cross-section of cultures and traditions to determine whether there are important similarities. Methods Thematic analysis was conducted with 15 creation stories from 11 traditions. Initial coding was reviewed to develop themes, which were then recursively applied to the stories to find further examples and refine definitions. The resulting 13 themes were then clustered into 4 categories. Results The diverse stories shared significant commonalities in their processes, elements, and implications. The first category is consciousness, which includes the themes of creator being, humans as co-creators, thought/mind, and one source. The second category is the elements, which includes the themes of water, light, and earth. The third category is opposites and similars, with no further subcategories. The fourth category is energy, which includes the themes of energy/vibration, breath, void, and time. Conclusions Surprising similarities across cultures point toward a model of reality in which consciousness is primary, preceding, and giving rise to physical form. All matter started as energy, and each part contains elements of the whole. The findings suggest that the divine, or universal consciousness, is contained in all matter, that consciousness may be eternal, and that the continuum of consciousness facilitates communication between humans, the divine, and all manifest forms.

title: Are we nursing the technologies? An ethnographic study of nurses’ tech work and its implications for well-being
authors: Paulien D'Huyvetter, Ellen Algera, Daantje Derks, Pascale Marie Le Blanc, Iris Wallenburg, Rik Wehrens
abstract: Healthcare systems across the world face persistent nursing shortages. Although technological innovations are widely promoted as solutions to rising workloads and staff shortages, they also generate additional, largely invisible forms of work. We examine nurses’ tech work: the unanticipated work nurses perform to keep hospital technologies functioning. Drawing on insights from Science and Technology Studies and Work and Organizational Psychology, we investigate the types of tech work nurses perform and their implications for nurses’ well-being. Based on ethnographically grounded observations, interviews, and focus groups conducted in a Dutch academic hospital, we identify eight types of tech work in nursing. For each type, we show tech work can negatively affect nurses’ well-being through hindrance demands and reduced perceptions of meaningfulness, particularly when combined with other demanding tasks. Our findings suggest that the challenge is not the deployment of more technologies, but their design and implementation in ways that minimize burdensome tech work and better support nurses’ care practices.

title: THE HORMUZ STRAIT DISRUPTION AND PAYMENT DELAYS IN INDIAN TRADE FINANCE: A Time-Series Analysis of Banking Sector Vulnerability (2019-2024)
abstract: The Hormuz Strait—through which 21% of global petroleum trade passes—experienced significant geopolitical tensions from 2019-2024, creating disruptions to maritime commerce and financial flows. This paper provides a detailed empirical analysis of how these disruptions affected payment cycles in Indian trade finance and banking. Using Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, port statistics, and transaction-level banking records (2019-2024, N=18,547 trade credit facilities), we employ time-series analysis, distributed lag models, and shock analysis to quantify the relationship between Hormuz disruptions and payment delays. Key findings: (1) Trade finance payment delays increased by an average of 8.3 days (95% CI: 6.1-10.5) following Hormuz tension announcements; (2) Letter of Credit (LC) issuance costs rose by 42-67 basis points; (3) Banks increased collateral requirements by 12-18%, contracting working capital availability by ₹4,200-6,800 crores; (4) The shock effect persisted for 90-120 days post-incident, with heterogeneous impacts across firm sizes (SMEs experienced 2.1x higher delays than large enterprises). Our analysis reveals that geopolitical shocks in maritime chokepoints generate significant financial friction in emerging market trade finance systems, with particular vulnerability among smaller firms lacking working capital buffers. We propose targeted policy interventions including development of trade credit insurance mechanisms, geographic diversification of banking relationships, and central bank communication frameworks for predictable intervention during crises.

title: Transforming Public Sector Corporations in Tanzania: A Capability-Based Framework for Addressing Persistent Governance, Financial, and Organizational Weaknesses
abstract: Public and Statutory Corporations (PSCs) remain important instruments for economic transformation, strategic investment, and public service delivery in developing economies. Governments establish PSCs to address market failures, provide essential services, support industrial development, and advance national economic objectives. However, despite growing interest in PSCs' governance, several gaps remain in existing literature. First, many studies focus primarily on ownership structures, privatization outcomes, and financial performance while paying limited attention to internal institutional capabilities. Second, existing performance assessments frequently identify weaknesses without developing systematic approaches for measuring recurring organizational constraints. Third, limited attention has been given to mechanisms that translate oversight findings into continuous organizational improvement. The study, therefore, addresses these gaps by developing the Public Sector Corporation Performance Weakness Index (PSC-PWI), an analytical framework designed to identify and measure recurring institutional weaknesses affecting PSCs' performance.

title: Psychological Readiness, Innovation Management, and the Adoption of Sustainable Agriculture: An Extended Theory of Planned Behaviour Model of Food Security among Smallholder Farmers in Climate-Vulnerable Bangladesh
authors: Md. Enamul Haque, M. Nasim Reza, Md. Nurul Islam Nepo, Syed M. Ali Reza, Md. Solaiman Chowdhury, Atikur Rahman
abstract: This study examines the psychological and managerial factors that influence the adoption of sustainable agricultural practices (SA) and household food security (FS) in climate-vulnerable regions of Bangladesh. Drawing on an integrated framework that combines the Extended Theory of Planned Behaviour (ETPB) with Innovation Diffusion Theory (IDT), the study analyses a refined sample of 380 smallholder farmers using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Unlike earlier models that confounded institutional and individual respondents, this study isolates the psychological readiness of primary producers by restricting the quantitative sample to active smallholders. The results show that climate change beliefs exert a significant positive effect on attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control, and that these socio-cognitive constructs in turn positively predict sustainable behavioural intention. Both behavioural intention and perceived behavioural control significantly influence the adoption of sustainable agriculture, which subsequently enhances food security. Individual innovation management further contributes to both the adoption of sustainable agriculture and food security outcomes. The findings underscore the importance of aligning the psychological readiness of individual farmers with the institutional readiness of the wider innovation system, offering a holistic basis for designing rural development strategies in climate-stressed agrarian economies.
